Counter-Strike 2 feels like a confident evolution of one of the most iconic competitive shooters ever made. It doesn’t try to reinvent Counter-Strike—and that’s exactly why it works so well.
The first thing you notice is the upgrade to the Source 2 engine. Maps look cleaner, lighting is more realistic, and animations feel smoother without losing the sharp clarity that competitive players rely on. Classic maps like Dust II and Mirage still feel familiar, but they’re more readable and alive than ever.
Gameplay-wise, CS2 stays true to the high-skill, low-margin formula that made CS legendary. Gunplay is still unforgiving and deeply rewarding, where precision, timing, and positioning matter more than flashy mechanics. The updated tick system and improved responsiveness make gunfights feel more consistent, which is crucial in a game where milliseconds decide rounds.
One of the biggest improvements is the smoke grenade rework. Smokes are now dynamic—bullets and grenades can temporarily clear them, and they interact naturally with the environment. This adds a fresh layer of strategy without overcomplicating the core gameplay, keeping matches tactical and exciting.
Sound design is another strong point. Audio cues are clearer and more directional, making it easier to track enemy movement and react intelligently. This enhances both casual play and high-level competitive matches.
CS2 isn’t perfect—some players may miss certain legacy features or feel the changes are subtle—but overall, it succeeds at modernizing Counter-Strike while respecting its roots. It’s a polished, competitive-focused shooter that rewards dedication, teamwork, and skill.
If you enjoy intense, tactical FPS games where improvement comes from mastery rather than upgrades, Counter-Strike 2 is absolutely worth your time.

This game was released twelve years ago, and its sequel only came out last year.
Even so, I want to strongly emphasize that this game is still a valid — and worthwhile — choice.

Over more than a decade, it has received continuous fixes and content updates, and it stands as a landmark in historical simulation, especially when it comes to Europe and the Middle East.
The Modd community is mature and active, and Paradox almost seems to enjoy watching players continue to expand and reshape the game.

Playing 5 right now often means dealing with glitches, even on highly tuned, high-end machines.
By contrast, 4 runs smoothly with very few issues — even on modern compact PCs.
Continuing to play this title isn’t a fallback or an act of avoidance.

There’s not much more to say.
Pick this up during a sale for around $10. You won’t regret it — graphics aside.

EU4 is the real Europa Universalis experience.
If you love war, conquest, and rewriting history from the Renaissance to Napoleon, this is the grand strategy game. Years of polish, systems that actually work together, and campaigns that stay fun for hundreds (or thousands) of hours.

EU4 might be an old veteran now, but it’s aged like fine wine. Tight pacing, satisfying campaigns, and warfare that feels rewarding instead of exhausting. It’s the grand strategy war game I’ve enjoyed the most, period.

EU5, on the other hand, feels like a chore disguised as a sequel.
I tried to like it. I really did. But it’s slow, clunky, and weirdly lifeless. The pacing is miserable, the UI/gamefeel is heavy, and so much of the time you’re not making bold strategic decisions, you’re fighting the interface and babysitting boring mechanics. It doesn’t feel “deeper,” it feels bloated.

Worst part? It loses what made EU4 addictive: momentum. In EU4, you’re planning wars, reacting to crises, building power, making moves. In EU5, you’re watching bars crawl, clicking through menus, and wondering when the game will finally let you play. It’s like they took a war-focused grand strategy classic and turned it into a sluggish resource-management simulator with extra steps.

And the playerbase (go to steam charts) tells the story better than any review: EU4 is still thriving because it’s simply more fun. EU5 being newer doesn’t matter if it’s less enjoyable.

If you’re choosing in 2026: play EU4.
EU5 can wait until it becomes a real game instead of a slow, frustrating prototype.

I love playing this game single player, and I hardly engage in the PvP portion of it at all.

The scavenging for loot and trying to survive is super satisfying. The ARC can be threatening if you make poor choices, but they become manageable and fun to take down once you have some gear and know their weaknesses.

The constant threat of other players makes the game exhilarating, but if you use voice chat and play friendly, you can frequently avoid conflict. There will be people who will try to kill you outright, and others who will pretend to be friendly so they can kill you easily once you drop your guard (rats).

The gameplay loop here is amazing, and I love that the game rewards you more for looting key spots quickly and trying to extract over running around and getting a bunch of kills.

They've managed to make something rare and special here in that it provides a fun extraction shooter for a reasonable price that is not infested with monetization. The gameplay is also unique in that it allows for both PVP and PVE playstyles to coexist through matchmaking that tends to put aggressive players together so they'll have a challenge while never completely eliminating the chance of a PVP encounter for the more PVE focused ones. They've pretty much nailed it and it would be hard to improve on this recipe as removing PVP entirely would eliminate a needed tension. The only point that I might recommend is considering letting people defend themselves without penalizing them by sending them into PVP matches after - it would give the players who start fights a slightly fairer challenge (the initiator has a huge advantage already) and the only people who won't want that are rats. So yeah, 9/10

while i know that extraction shooters are not for everyone, even me, this game has brought back my love for gaming. I can't begin to describe how many times I was grinning ear to ear, feeling anxious, cautious, made friends, helped out fellow raiders that I'll probably never see again. Even had moments in being able to be a hero for a raider that was backstabbed or knocked by arc. I don't get to play as often as I'd like to but this game is rent free in my mind. I'd recommend you take your time with this game. enjoy the learning curve. learn what weapon's you like. Figure out what type of raider you want to be and lean into it. There is constant debate about what the true purpose of this game is, PVP? PVE? but the reality is this game is truly PVEVP. it is what you make of it. at first I hated being killed by an extraction camper or being backstabbed and it still can upset me, but honestly its forced me to be better. check my surroundings better, be more cautious of other players. the tension of the game is real and the ai enemies are actually a threat. listen you will be killed and lose good gear, legendary gear even. times where you die to the AI. times you team up with a random player. times you play instruments and vibe out on the topside. There will be moments where you will be knocked but you're still laughing so hard. times where you save others and they save you. even times where the AI enemies will save you by accident( or not?). this game is a game of extremely high high's, and low lows. its a gamble every match. and those memorable gaming moments around almost every corner. This is Arc Raiders. I'm a gamer at heart and always have been. This is the first game i ever left a review on. This game revitalized gaming for me. it won't be everyone's cup of tea but i say give it a shot. this is a hell of a game for its price ($40) and it is only getting started. i hope embark takes this momentum and really takes it somewhere legendary. i honestly didn't know what I was gonna write but i can honestly keep going. i really just want to boot up and launch into topside . i hope this review helped capture the feeling that this game is and I hope to see you Topside raiders.

I used to enjoy this game - I have over 100 hours and have hit level 75. That being said, there are two frustrating aspects of this game that make me feel like playing is a waste of my time.

The most frustrating aspects of this game are the late-game spawns, and spawning in at the edge of the maps. If I spawn in a map with less than 25 minutes left, all the loot will be gone. If I spawn in at the edge of the map, by the time I get to loot locations, all the loot will be gone.

I used to think getting shot in the back by rats was the worst aspect of this game, but to be honest spawning in late and realizing I have to run all the way to an elevator just to get out of the match is the worst aspect of this game. I wouldn't mind late game spawns if loot respawned, or if I had the option to leave the match immediately with my gear. You see, if you want to leave the match right away, your only current option is to "surrender" which means you lose all the equipped gear you have.

So when I realize I've spawned in late, I have to spend the next 2-3 minutes running to an elevator, dodging robots and rats while using up items to run quickly across the map. Then I load back into the hub area and hit "play" again hoping that I won't end up in another late game spawn.

I usually do. 

Trying to find blueprints turns into a constant cycle of this and it's extremely frustrating. I wouldn't recommend this to new players because you run into this wall of frustration end game. There isn't even a lot to do right now, and I understand there is end-game content on the way but right now the game just feels frustrating to play. I don't want to login and feel like I've wasted my time.

Arc Raiders is game that brings me mixed feelings, but in its current state, I can't honestly recommend playing it. But let's start with the good.

The Pros:

Arc Raiders premise is excellent, if not original. Earth was razed by war and the surface has become a barren land, hostile to life itself. The story arch of Arc Raiders focuses on an underground settlement known as Speranza, where survivors scramble through and gather hoping to survive as they prepare to resurface. However, they found that the surface is not quiet either, a variety of automatons, machines called "ARC", patrol the ruins of what remains topside, and they are hostile, it seems their mission and endeavor to eliminate any remaining humans. With this in mind, groups of "Raiders",one of which is you, the player, organise to raid the surface and scrunge up any supplies, intel and tech they can get their hands on, to both survive, learn more about the enemy and their motivations, and prepare to fight back. 

This is pretty great - and even moreso when the gameplay itself, is great as well. Technical issues with server connectivity aside, the controls are responsive, the weapons are varied and have each their own identity, strengths and weaknesses, and the combat feels fluid and action packed. Arc Raiders is a beautiful extraction shooter, with clean, responsive controls, and an interesting premise to back it all.


The cons:

While the game was originally devised as PvE game, probably similar to Helldivers (in fact, the reward system seems to be a shameless copy from Helldivers) at one point they made the decision to add PvP to it, but unfortunately, that must have also skewed their development direction too, because the game has no content whatsoever. It does have several maps, but there are no progression systems. No difficulties, tiers, nothing. The first time you load the first map you ever play, as a level 1 greenhorn with a default pistol will be exactly the same map wiith the same enemy dificulty, density, and rewards as the map 2.500 you enter 1000 hours into the game.  

The gameplay loop is setup much like a  mobile gacha game, and its designed to fire off your dopamine receptors and create artifcial addiction at every turn. Every container you open gives off lively slot machine sounds, with increasingly higher pitched gratifying jackpot sounds when you get higher rarity items, that in truth are not that rare. Every run you'll end up with more purple (epic) + blue (rare) items in your inventory than gray (common)+ green (uncommon), but that will keep you chasing those slot machine sounds, to create the artificial addiction that may even fool you for some time before you stop to think if you're actually having fun, or just hoarding things of the colors the game makes chirpier slot machine sounds for.  Case in point, the best weapons of the game are the starting ones, white and green (common and uncommon) both for PvP and PvE, while the epic (purple) are widely known to be some of the worst weapons in the game. But the purple ones give out a jackpot slot machine sound when you find them, and you'll see people getting super hyped about getting one, just to stash it and never use it because a starting Stitcher gun is better anyway.

 When your dopamine receptors are about to blow, you will realize there is nothing to play for. There's no PvE progression, difficulty, or systems that incentivize getting better at the game, that reward player skill or dediucation. And then you'll find yourself basically playing a glorified fetch simulator, just hoarding your 7th "Hyperconductor tape" item your stash, just incase one day one NPC gives you a fetch quest about getting one, and saves you the trouble of having to go get it then.  

I haven't spoken of the PvP side of things, because I don't even consider this game to be PvP. A hundred percent of the player kills happen because someone gets the jump on someone else and kills them before they can fight back, or they're so bad at pointing their crosshair that the person being shot turns around and kills them back. There's no tactical gameplay, no nuance, no player skill expression, and none of it is supported by any ranking systems, matchmaking, ladders or anything of the kind. It's mostly if you';re cool with trying to kill someone to get their loot instead of trying to find your own loot, go for it. Nothing stops you, and nothing supports you. In the end, it doesn't matter, whatever they had, you could have gotten yourself, and they won't miss it either, since loot is abundant, and there's very very little you can do with it. 



Conclusion: 

This is a game to keep in the radar, if it survives this phase where it's more of a server performance stress test than anything else and they make a game out of it. I realise people can think differently about what is fun or what is not, to me, right now, Arc Raiders is a shell of game that offers nothing beyond being popular due to streamers promoting it, and creating a "monkey see monkey do" effect that will die sooner or later, unless it gets turned into a real game. They need to add content, in all fronts. Tiers, difficulties, meaningful rewards, progression, ladders, systems, proper matchmaking; both in PvP and PvE, make it feel like you're playing for something more than looting items that make slot machine sounds when you pick them up just to fire up your dopamine receptors in the cheapest possible way. 

If they don't, at least I played 80 hours of this game so you don't have to. Consider using your hard earned money and your limited time in a better way, good chance you won't regret.

After 540+ hours, it’s safe to say ARC Raiders hasn’t just hooked me-it’s lived rent-free in my head. The game absolutely nails that high-stakes extraction loop where every decision matters and every run feels like it could turn legendary or disastrous in seconds. Gunplay is tight and satisfying, movement is smooth and responsive, and the constant PvE/PvP tension keeps your heart rate up from drop-in to extraction.

The world is gritty, atmospheric, and full of quiet dread, pulling you in without ever holding your hand. ARC enemies feel genuinely dangerous, not like filler content, and player encounters are unpredictable in the best way -sometimes it’s a tense standoff, other times it’s pure chaos. Progression feels rewarding, skill-based, and earned, and the deeper your map knowledge and game sense get, the more the game opens up.

Where ARC Raiders truly shines is in its moment-to-moment choices: push your luck or play it safe, take the fight or disappear into the environment, extract now or risk it all for better loot. It creates unforgettable highs, painful losses, and endless “one more run” moments. It’s intense, addictive, and incredibly rewarding-and clearly, it worked on me.

[h1]Not Recommended[/h1]

[b]I hate that I’m writing this.[/b] I loved Arc Raiders. I still do, in a messed-up way. That’s what makes this so painful.

After [b]160+ hours[/b], I finally uninstalled.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Matchmaking That Punishes You for Playing[/h2]

The matchmaking design is [b]genuinely awful[/b]. The game actively punishes you for [i]defending yourself[/i].

You get a few calm, friendly raids:
[list]
[*]People coexist
[*]You loot
[*]You progress
[/list]

Then a rat camps an extract. You shoot back because you need the loot for a quest.

[b]Congratulations.[/b]
The game now decides:
[i]“YOU SHOT BACK, SO YOU MUST WANT PVP.”[/i]

From here on out:
[list]
[*]Kill the rat → sweatlord PvP hell
[*]Don’t kill the rat → lose loot, time, and progress
[*]Either way → you’re punished
[/list]

There’s zero nuance. Zero context. Zero care.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Bugs That Literally Kill You[/h2]

Not funny bugs.
Not “haha early access jank” bugs.

[b]Run-ending. Loot-deleting. Time-wasting bugs.[/b]

Add in constant server instability and it genuinely feels like the game is fighting you at every step.

[h3]Spawns Are TERRIBLE[/h3]

Enemy spawns are a disaster:
[list]
[*]Awful early-game spawns
[*]Even worse mid-game spawning
[*]Enemies popping in where they absolutely shouldn’t
[/list]

It kills immersion. It kills fairness. Sometimes it just straight-up kills [i]you[/i].

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Loot System: Clunky, Dishonest, and Insulting[/h2]

The game tells you:
[i]“Go to red areas for higher-tier loot.”[/i]

Reality:
[list]
[*]Same Burletta
[*]Again
[*]And again
[*]And again
[/list]

Every. Single. Time.

That gun is so useless you’d do more damage [b]sneezing[/b] on a Raider than actually shooting them. High risk, zero reward. The loot doesn’t feel connected to the map info or progression at all.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Worst Part? It Could Be Amazing[/h2]

When this game is good, it’s [b]beautiful[/b]:
[list]
[*]Atmosphere
[*]Tension
[*]Concept
[/list]

When everything lines up, it [i]hits hard[/i].

But when it’s bad—and that’s more often than not—it [b]SUUUUCKS[/b].

Bugs, bad spawns, broken matchmaking logic, ignored community feedback, and systems that punish you for playing naturally.

This game has [b]insane potential[/b]. Watching it fail to reach it hurts more than if it were just bad from the start.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]

[b]I LOVE this game.[/b] Don’t get it twisted.

If they:
[list]
[*]Fix the bugs
[*]Stabilize the servers
[*]Rethink matchmaking
[*]Make loot and spawns actually make sense
[/list]

I would [b]GLADLY[/b] come back.

But as it stands?

[b]Don’t waste your time.[/b]
[b]Don’t waste your money.[/b]

ARK Raiders is an absolute blast and lives up to the hype, It's one of those games that has that lightning trapped in a bottle type feel. Currently the most popular extraction shooter to date and there are many reasons for its success, From it's launch the gameplay, visuals, the amount of people showcasing the game through streaming is what made it's popularity skyrocket. It's shares similar traits as most extractions shooters like stash/inventory management and PvPvE. But there is something special about this one, Gunplay and movement mechanics feel satisfying and smooth, each map does a great job of setting the tone and atmosphere as the world feels alive with it's vibrant sci-fi visuals and dynamic weather that affects gameplay. It's great to play solo or with friends, You will encounter other Raiders not knowing who is truly friendly or not. I've went through countless raids and hours of play time without it feeling too grindy so it offers a ton of replay value.. It's not often when games like this release and I believe the developers at Embark studios have something special on their hands for years to come. Whether it's the slick PvP combat fighting players or taking down ARK for more of a PvE approach, I highly recommend if you are a fan of shooters in general, You don't even need to be a fan of extraction shooters to enjoy this game because once you sink your teeth into it, You will understand why it has been so hyped since it's release.

This work feels completely derivative compared to The Finals. The fact that Arc Raiders is far more popular than The Finals (another game by the same company) blows my mind. The gameplay of Arc Raiders is basically a steam punk copy-paste of the extraction shooter genre.

It's nothing special -- aside from one key feature: aggression based MMR. This is the only reason that I continue to play this game. It is quite fascinating to see how different shooters are when they make matches based on whether or not you like to PvP. When I play solo, I do not fight humans. And I get into the most chill multiplayer lobbies I've ever seen, where there is little to no PvP violence, and it is common for people to talk to strangers and help one another find the loot that we're looking for. When I play with my friends (I come from a fairly hard-core competitive shooter background) the experience is entirely different, and nothing special -- it's shoot on sight (with strategy and coordination), just like any other extraction shooter.

Originality 1/10, story 1/10, weapons 0.5/10, the fact that it's TPP instead of FPP -5/10, having to wait for a fake loading screen to see loot even though computers are fast these days -10/10, decent default mouse sensitivity 7/10, aggression based MMR 9/10.

In my opinion, this game is terrible compared to The Finals, which is one of the most innovative and interesting shooters of the past decade. However, the unique MMR system makes this game worth experiencing if you enjoy PVE gameplay. I hope to see this MMR system adopted into other games, which will make this game a cool piece of OG gaming history worth playing to know, but not worth playing on repeat.

ARC Raiders delivers a strong first impression through its atmosphere and core concept. The world feels heavy and hostile, and the constant threat of the ARC machines creates real tension during gameplay. Unlike many shooters that focus purely on fast action, ARC Raiders emphasizes caution, teamwork, and survival, which makes every encounter feel meaningful. The sound design and visuals do a great job of selling the idea that humanity is no longer in control, especially when exploring the surface and hearing distant mechanical movements.

The cooperative aspect is one of the game’s biggest strengths. Working with teammates to scavenge resources and decide when to fight or retreat adds depth and encourages communication. However, this reliance on teamwork may feel punishing for solo players, as mistakes can be costly and progress can feel slow without coordination. At times, combat can feel unforgiving, especially when resources are limited, which may discourage new players.

Overall, ARC Raiders stands out for its immersive sci-fi setting and tense survival mechanics. With some balancing improvements and clearer onboarding for beginners, it has the potential to become a memorable and rewarding cooperative experience for players who enjoy strategic, high-risk gameplay.

ARC Raiders wants you to believe it’s a tactical extraction shooter about teamwork, strategy, and survival. What it actually is: a beautifully rendered anxiety simulator where giant murder-robots exist solely to ruin your day and humble you in front of strangers.

You drop in feeling confident. Slick gunplay. Clean UI. “This feels good,” you think. That’s mistake number one. Within minutes, a mech the size of a small office block notices you breathing and deletes your entire squad with military-grade disinterest. No cutscene. No warning. Just instant obliteration and a loading screen that quietly asks why you bothered.

The PvE enemies are relentless, the PvP players are worse, and both are united by a shared goal: making sure you extract with absolutely nothing. ARC Raiders has perfected the art of letting you almost succeed. You’ll be one corridor from extraction, pockets full, heart racing... then a third party shows up like a tax audit with legs.

Every run teaches valuable life lessons such as:
• Never get attached to loot
• Trust no teammate named “SoloKing”
• Hope is a resource you should not invest in

The maps are gorgeous, which is ironic because you’ll spend most of your time face-down on them. The sound design is so good you can hear your impending death approaching from three zip codes away. The tension is real. So is the disappointment.

And yet… you queue again. Because when it clicks—when the squad syncs, the shots land, and you extract clean... you feel unstoppable. Briefly. Until the next run reminds you who’s actually in charge.

ARC Raiders doesn’t just punish mistakes. It punishes confidence.
It doesn’t hate you.
It just doesn’t care if you survive.

Would I recommend it?
Yes, if you enjoy stress, teamwork arguments, and the slow erosion of joy.

One more run. Surely this one goes well.

Arc Raiders is a highly social extraction shooter with adaptive matchmaking, and these features are probably what makes it stand out the most within its own extraction shooter genre. 

Unlike Tarkov or Hunt:showdown this game isn't trying to be stressful, competetive, none of that. The experience here started as PvE where players would need to work together to overcome machines that were stat-padded beyond belief to force teamwork. With the right preperation/loadout you can still solo whatever problems you run into. The game definitely allows for work smarter not harder solutions to almost any problem.

The game has a matchmaking system that puts like-minded players together. If you join lobbies and always shoot first, other players in your lobbies will also always shoot you first. If you never PvP and avoid combat at all costs you'll see tons of CoOp players and empty lobbies. 
This feeds into the PvE side of the game. Some people do want PvP but a lot of players just want to create experiences. This is similar to Sea Of Thieves in how the game can play. The PvP exists so any player can play "their part" but it's not like the game uses this as a foundation for your decisions. There really isn't much reason to kill other players unless you outright enjoy the PvP or enraging casual players who don't want to deal with it. (Most common complaint about this game I've seen is Non Pvpers being forced to PvP. I can't relate because the matchmaking actually seems to work REALLY WELL. Are these "friendlies" killing other people in their spare time then complaining about the consequences maybe?)

Anyway first glance the game seems like another third person extraction shooter. The difference is how hard the devs are promoting players to work together or finding ways to keep the ones who will apart from the ones who won't. I don't know if trying to cater to two communities can work long-term but we'll see how that goes. 

Gun balance can be pretty bad but small team. There's one particularly bad purple weapon that uses expensive ammo, fire fast, and deals real low damage. The cost on firing in excessive for no reason and isn't even backed by good damage. I'll just run any other rifle or handcannon thanks.
Bad balance relates to PvP, not PvE. I do not think balance can be bad enough to matter in PvE here. You're likely going to be running explosives/tools anyway. 

The weakest part of the game is the lame-ass quests. It's basically just Tarkov, Find objective, hold E to interact, extract. One of the weakest part of almost all extraction shooters are these boring time wasting objectives that exist to make you feel a sesne of progression so you hopefully won't just quit if the gameplay loop gets stale/boring. 
These quests are never the reason I keep playing, and I have my doubts I'll even complete them if 100%ing achievements doesn't require it.

When Ark Ascends the Extraction shooter genre and adds RPG elements (The right kind, like from Witchfire) so we can take unique items found in-raid to another raid and use it at a specific map location to summon a 1-time boss or similar mechanics then I'll start crediting them for interesting quests/objectives. For now the replay value comes down to you and the community though.

ARC Raiders has put my faith back into humanity. Not just because the subject matter is us against the machines, James Cameron can tell you about that, but because when people are given the choice to shoot or not, they generally don't. This game, at it's core, is about collecting loot and making it home safely, which is easier said than done. If you like running away from giant mechs, having your butt clench up real tight, and watching your fellow man (or woman) save that same tight butt as you both laugh while the hatch is closing, this is for you.

Man, I actually hate Arc Raiders. I'm trying to remember another game where my interest was as flatlined as that game. It's kinda like with movies, where the worst thing a movie can be is completely middle-of-the-road boring, almost like horseshoe theory, where the worse it gets the more interesting it gets.

I think Ark: Survival and Dying Light come close though... and both have really shoe-horned in loot-finding, crafting, and skill trees, "hold button to fill circle to *then* be displayed a list of literal trash you've found to then click through" search mechanics. Busy work for the sake of """being addicting""" to keep you playing because the game's main focus is real-time mass multiplayer, where if the player base dies, then the game dies. In 5-10 years, no one will remember this game, no one will talk about it.

Also they all have the "menu hell" that every modern game has. Reminds me of the worst aspects of Ni-Oh, or Quake Champions, or  ANY battle royale game, but with none of the good aspects. I feel like a lot of people view gaming as "just something to do to fill the void", so they love all this kind of sh*t. Which, to be clear, is why modern gaming is the way it is. Because something like what a bunch of more esoteric indie games (UFO 50, for example) go for is too... "jagged", polarizing, experimental. People like the familiar & generic, they don't want to be challenged.

You might say you could just ignore the looting & menu hell altogether, and just roll a free load out, sure, but the core gameplay is still uninspired run-of-the-mill 3rd person shooting action with cut-and-paste exploration. Regardless, you most certainly will need to engage with the loot autism on a long enough time line. You can buy weapons & gear from the store, but you'd need to get money from selling the loot. You'd save time by memorizing/looking up what you can craft from that loot or upgrade from that loot (or break down to recyclable sub-trash) to save money, since you're already hunting that same loot to get money anyway. So you'd need to memorize/look-up what to keep, sell, and recycle. Then use your extra money to shortcut where it makes sense. And you need to do all this since when you inevitably run into aggressive players, the upgraded, better guns are just flat out better. You lose your good stuff if you die, so you then will need to do brain-dead busy work loot runs. In addition to all this, you get EXP from looting. You need the EXP to climb the skill tree to get basic "More stamina" "run faster" "suck ass-hole less" "take less damage from explosions" BS that all the people who are aggressive and have already sank hundreds of hours into the game already have, along with their better guns.

The circular logic here is crazy. If anyone likes this, that's fine. I just struggle to think of a game I'd rather play less, which is **not** and exaggeration. It's the gaming equivalent of making license plates in a prison work line, or turning big rocks into little rocks.

MODERN GAMING, EVERYONE! Oh, how the mighty have fallen. I guess I have the entirety of the rest of my library to play instead, so I'm golden.

Arc Raiders is an extraction shooter. It says exactly what it is on the box and you get exactly what you buy from it. 

The issue is the fundamental flaw with extraction shooter genre, and whether you can over come this flaw and still enjoy it.

Gear Inequity. Due to how the game is structured you have to win to get good gear. Die? You lose everything, Even if you have 2 other players in your squad win, dying means you lose. Have a good gun? Die and it's gone, make a new one. Made a new gun? Die and it's gone. Now you are down 2. If you don't win you continue to lose and continue to lose gear to actually run with. 

Then the game gets to a point where the only people left playing are people with better guns. And since guns in this game are Statistically better when upgraded, and will kill you FASTER than your weaker guns, you are now ALWAYS playing with a disadvantage. Ope you just died to a guy with a gun that killed you in 2 hits. He has 6x times your shields and was holding a corner you could never push. Now you have no gear. 

The game attempts to allieviate this by giving you free loadouts, but this doesn't actually stop the problem. Free loadouts will almost never beat upgraded guns. 

You are now in an endless cycle of attempting to get enough garbage crafting materials out just to make a gun, or a kit, or something. 

Allow me to showcase an event that happened in game.

My group was attempting to do a fast extraction, with free kits, to grab 2 items to upgrade the automatic loot farmer. We got to extraction, and another team was there. We pleaded over the microphone: "Stop we literally only have peaches and lemons." The other team still used 6 grenades and 4 mags to dump into us to prevent us from leaving. They got 3 half damaged free kits and no consumables, and 4 peaches and a lemon. Was it funny? Sure, did we have to do the same suicide run 6 more times so 3 of us could upgrade our loot generator? Sure. But the fun is gone after a while. 

Is the game good? Yes, I would say its an amazing extraction shooter.

Can I recommend it? No.

A Masterpiece Smothered by PvP Extraction Tropes

​Current Status: Mixed / Thumbs Down (Pending Improvements)

​I want to love this game. I’ve spent hundreds of hours in this world, and the core of what Embark has built is genuinely special. However, the recent shift in direction—leaning heavily into a "Tarkov-lite" PvP mindset—is systematically dismantling the atmosphere and camaraderie that made the game unique.

​The Good: Atmosphere, Design, and Moments of Humanity
​Visual & World Direction: The art style and visual fidelity are top-tier. The "unknowing" challenges and the way the world presents itself keep the gameplay loop fresh.
​The ARC AI: The mechanical threat feels imposing and intelligent, making every encounter with the machines a true challenge.
​Organic Camaraderie: There is nothing like the feeling of saving an overwhelmed player with a defib or building trust with a stranger. My real-world hunting skills actually feel applicable here—tracking, sneaking, and picking the right moment to move.
​The Critical Issues: The "Tarkov" Shadow
​Inventory Chaos: The inventory system feels like it was designed by a team that doesn’t communicate. Stash space is far too limited, and the lack of proper stacking for basic materials makes maintenance a chore rather than a mechanic. Putting a "value" on a loadout feels meaningless when the gear balance is this skewed.
​PvP Toxicity: Shifting the focus to hard PvP has invited a "heartless" community. The sense of mystery is being replaced by "ratting"—players just waiting at doors or extracts to kill you in the back for loot they didn't work for. It’s unbalanced, cheap, and kills the PvE design.
​The Gear Disconnect: High-tier gear is too costly to maintain and often underperforms compared to "cheap" meta weapons. It feels like high-tier gear is a letdown, while low-tier gear allows PvP players to "stat-check" everyone without risk.
​Mechanical Imbalance & Augment Design
​The Shield Problem: There is a massive lack of balance between Augments and Shields. Seems like only combat and tactical augments will be giving medium shields. All MK3 aug should allow for Medium Shields. Being punished for using a looting mk3 that doesnt have a med shield makes me feel like im just goop for pvp players. 
It makes no sense that a high-tier looting mk3 augment build forces you into a weak defense, making you a walking target for PvP "chops."
​Augment Logic: The new augments feel like "band-aids" for base game issues. One lets you put a gun in a safe pocket—which should have been a base feature—while the unlimited defib has such a long cooldown (4 mins) that it’s useless in late-match entries.
​The "Late Entry" Trap: The CEO has suggested that entering a match late (15–20 mins in) leads to "better loot," but in reality, you just find empty boxes and plastic because everything has been picked clean. It feels like a nudge to stop looting and start killing other players for their bags—a total pivot from the "pioneer" PvE roots.

​Proposed Solutions for Embark
​Separate Servers: Stop treating us as data points. Give us a choice: PvE-only servers for those who want to immerse in the world and the machine threat, and PvPvE servers for those who want the sweat.
​Standardize Extracts: Get rid of the randomized hatch times. Make all extracts consistent so "rats" can't just camp the only open exit.
​Self-Revive: Give players a single self-revive chance. In a world where even "friendly" players are being pushed to loot your body, we need a way to get back up once without relying on a toxic community.
​Balance the MK3s: Give the MK3 Augments all a Medium Shield. If it’s meant to be a high-tier survivability build, let us actually survive.
​Final Word
​Embark is currently leaning into a crowd that tells PvE players to "go play Minecraft." If the devs continue to ignore the community that fell in love with the original PvE vision in favor of chasing a rude, PvP-focused meta, they will lose the heart of their player base. I have the passion to stay, but not if my opinion as a dedicated player doesn't matter.

A game I have been waiting years to play, when it was still supposed to be PVE. 

The world is beatiful and breathtaking, from lush swamps to concreate and desert, I cought myself many times just enjoying the view. The scale and monumentality of the loacations topside seems intimidating at first but quickly makes you feel at home. Reminds me a bit of Denis Villeneuve portreyal of Dune, looking at you Spaceport. You can even find some cinematographers directing short scenes in the game, that's how you know it's great. The game offers 5 unique maps, each with different environments, challenges and threats, what works on one may fail you on others, that makes things interesting and rewards those who adapt. Add seasonal and permanent events like electromagnetic storm or night raids and double the variety.

The Arc are a threat that command respect and fear, they are no joke and evolve their tactics alongside the Raiders who balance betweeen prey and hunter. When possible you pick your fights, sometimes taking cover and hiding is the only way out when alarmed Arc call for backup with their terrifing electronic howls and circle around you like wolves. You can hide but you can't run, they will get you and the next thing you see is Speranza.

As last humans under mechine terror we are not defenceless, the world provides us with diffferent kinds of weapons to fight the Arc, from simple firearms like handguns, SMGs, shotguns and bolt or lever action rifles to granade launchers and energy weapons. The arsenal of gadgets, mines and grenades deserves a whole different chapter as their use cases are fueled by human creativity alone, even the devs were impressed - flying deadline :0 

We are not alone. More often then not you will encounter other riders who like you want to survive and get back home with what they managed fill their backpacks with, maybe you will help each other fighting the Arc, share supplies, extract together and be friends, maybe. 

Maybe they will betray you when you type in the security codes in the elevator just before your return to speranza, laughting at how gullible and naive you are and they are right. There are many ways to protect yourself from Arc but what saves you from other riders are your instincts, raiders will lie to you, they will gain your trust and hit you when you least expect it, you will learn how and who to trust the hard way and the lessons are punishing. You get to know yourself a lot in situations like that, will you preemptively kill a "friendly" just because they feel off? Will you kill another to save yourself? What if there is a witness? Will you kill them too? Will you kill out of fear? Or will you die becase you are brave enough to trust?

That was what the good part, now the bad and ugly.
The core of the game has not yet crystallized so it's a gamble, it has potential to become a great game over the years but right now Embark Studios is not sure what their game is supposed to be. After few hundred hours it's safe to say the endgame is nonexistent, play loop becomes either boring or frustrating, excietment wears off, novelty fizzles down and all that's left is stash full weapons that are prohibitively expansive to repair. Freeloadaout was initially good idea that was implemented in a way that serves only cheaters, who by the way just recived 3 strikes before permanently banned. 

Close to no content updates, too much focus on skin microtransactions, timegated events, lackluster projects, dozens of tabs and menus just to gear up for a game where a freeloadout kills you.
Want to kill a Bastion or Bombardier in an epic fight? Forget it, after first agro nearby raiders will make sure you are not getting out alive and even if you do a rat will kill you at extraction.

If you like PVE this is not a game for you.
If you like PVP this is not a game for you.

Arc Raiders is a great game – it really is.

I really adore the world, the maps with its love for detail and hundreds of corners to discover. The exploration, the discoveries, the gunplay, the design of the ARCs – I love everything about it.
I had 70 hours of mostly loads of fun – and this certainly worth a recommendation.

But … As much as I love the game for its PvE content: I personally don’t like that you are sometimes forced into PvP situations. Even if you are not interested in it. The game is designed like this, and I assume it’s meant to bring the “extra spice” … the “extra thrill” as you can never feel safe.

Going into a map with heavy equipment. Spending 20-25 minutes to battle bigger ARCs and then getting camped/killed by a “Free Loadout” Raider at the extraction point, who has not taken any risk entering the map feels unpleasant. For me personally, this is not the “extra thrill” … it’s the “extra downer”.

I might come back, if there should be a PvE mode, but I have decided to stop playing – leaving the game for good. To all players buying and playing the game: Enjoy! It’s a great game – especially if you’re into the “extra thrill” described above.

I decided to pick the game up because I heard good things from people I trust.  I was worried because I don't typically play extraction shooters due to literally the core mechanic of getting killed and losing everything in your inventory.

My first round, I was absolutely terrified. I hid in a bush for 25 minutes and then sprinted into a elevator under duress.

My second round, I completed a mission, hid in a building for 10 minutes, then died because a Wasp found me and called a second Wasp, which I was completely unprepared for. I really should have looked up gameplay before I bought this game.

After several more rounds, I started encountering other players, which was also initially terrifying. I didn't really know the communication meta and expected people to just walk up and blast me.  However, I quickly got the hang of things and begun the early game resources grind to upgrade your crafting stations and get better gear. Player interaction was never quite co-operative, but people would run by, flash their light or use a greeting emote, and be on their way.  I was finally getting confident in the gameplay, especially in knowing where things were on the Dam level. I could get into a round, fill up my inventory with goodies, and hit an escape elevator whenever it suited me.

Then, one game, someone just walked up and shot me in the face. Oh yeah, this is a PvP game. I stared long and hard at my empty inventory. Why did I do this to myself? Hours of progress gone in an instant of blind trust. Anyway, I queued up again and got all my stuff back quicker the next time around.

Overall I think it's a good game because I stepped outside my comfort zone and was rewarded. I think the  artwork and environment design are great and best of all, it's enjoyable to use your weapon. There are some minor issues here and there but that's how it goes. I think crafting could be designed a little better, I found myself having to click in a lot of different places to get what I wanted. Also, unless there's something I missed about the Blueprint mechanic, it seems like I am waiting on random chance to get the Blueprints I need to reliably create and maintain my gear. I find myself with a lot of raw resources that I can't spend.

I may never truly embrace the extraction shooter PvPvE gameplay style, but I feel like parts of the perfect game for me are in here somewhere. Hey, don't shoot!

Gameplay Vibes

• 	The firefights hit that sweet spot between “cinematic” and “why is everything exploding again.”
• 	Every encounter turns into a full‑blown platoon operation except with more screaming and fewer safety briefs.
• 	The physics engine deserves a medal for how many times it launched one of us into low orbit.

Team Dynamics

Playing with an Army team adds a special flavor:
• 	Someone is always trying to flank… even when flanking is physically impossible.
• 	Someone else is hoarding ammo “for later,” then panicking when the ARC drop a titan on us.
• 	And there’s always that one guy who insists he’s “just testing the fall damage.”
Honestly, the game should give bonus XP for “maintaining unit cohesion despite questionable decision‑making.”

The ARC

The ARC enemies feel like they were designed by someone who asked, “What if robots were angry about everything?”
They swarm, they snipe, they drop from the sky like they’re late for formation.
We respect them.
We hate them.
We keep fighting them anyway.

Highlights from 40 Hours

• 	Accidentally discovering that teamwork does matter when we actually try it.
• 	Perfectly timed revives that felt more heroic than anything we’ve done in real life.
• 	That one mission where everything went wrong but we somehow pulled it off and acted like it was intentional.

 Final Verdict

Arc Raiders with the squad is chaotic, hilarious, and surprisingly tactical.
It’s the closest thing to a field exercise without the heat, the sand, or someone yelling about accountability formation.

If the next 40 hours are anything like the first, the ARC don’t stand a chance though our comms discipline probably does.

I’m about 15 hours in, and I’m still kind of mixed. The PvE + PvP setup keeps every run tense — you never really know how it’s going to play out, and that unpredictability is what makes it fun. When it works, it really works. The game looks and sounds great, the guns feel good, and the atmosphere does a lot of the heavy lifting. There are moments where everything clicks and it pulls you in hard.

The best parts are easily the unplanned player interactions. I’ve been trash-talked and wiped, had clean extractions, and even been saved at the last second by random squads just doing their thing. Extraction camping shows up a lot, and on top of that, load-in times can be rough — sometimes we spawn late with only around 15 minutes left, which is a huge disatvantage when it comes to looting the spots you need to farm.

The game also leans pretty hard on AI, and that’s where PvP starts to feel off. Drones jump in forcing loud engagements that burn your ammo, give away your position, and leave you weak before the player fight even gets going. When it finally wraps up, it’s less about aim or movement and more about who still has resources left. By the time you reach extraction, you’re usually worn down — which is exactly when players who’ve been camping the extract all raid step in and clean up with their full loadouts. It makes surviving the run feel less rewarding. If drones are meant to create chaos, it’d make way more sense for them to pressure extraction zones so campers actually have to play the game.

Cosmetics are also insanely overpriced, and while the core loop can be fun, it starts to feel repetitive faster than it should — loot, craft, repeat.

Overall, it’s not a bad game, but it’s also not quite hitting what I expected yet. It’s already given me some genuinely memorable moments, and if you’re into tense extraction games with strong atmosphere and player-driven chaos, there’s definitely something here — just go in knowing there’s a lot of camping and heavier AI pressure than you might want right now.

[h1]100 hours in a casual game is exceptional, for me[/h1]

Arc Raiders is an extraction shooter, that gives you the opportunity to decide if you shoot other players. You can play alone, or with up to three friends. The rules are simple, [b]just survive.[/b] At the end, it only matters that you are safe with your loot at home.

[h2]Why I like this game[/h2]
[b]It is nearly perfect. I mean, nothing can be perfect, but Arc Raiders is unique.[/b]

The thing that makes this game so good for me is because it gives me a special feeling that I can´t describe. I mean that feeling when I randomly find an Aphelion blueprint, or I meet other Raiders. The emotions and actions that happen during a game are the things that make me play this game. I really enjoyed when I had to laugh, or even if I raged, just everything. I can´t rate the graphics because I don´t play enough games to really understand them.

[h3]Game experience[/h3]

You queue in a game and you always have a different mood. Just imagine you have 10 Wolfpacks with you, and you hope that nobody shoots you. Maybe you are chill and run a free loadout. Or you take your Tempest with you, that you have found last round. Your mood already changes before the round starts. That is literally amazing, I think it is an unnoticed detail that many people don´t see.
You search for good stuff and then another player appears. This is the moment when you need to make a decision. You either shoot him or you don´t. Trust me, thats not as that easy as it sounds. Many players are friendly, but be aware there are a few that pretend to be are friendly and then shoot you in the back. Of course, if you are in PVP lobbies, this is something different but in most lobbies a few will shoot and a few won´t. And really you will feel bad, if you eliminate a friendly player. This makes you think twice before shooting at someone. But if you think to long and the player is hostile. Well then it is over for you. Keep that in mind.

[i]"Arc Raiders it lets you play how you want and not how the the game wants you to play"[/i]
Random Raider that I meet.

Summary: You search for loot and need to make decidions that change the end of the match.

I really don´t want to spoiler to much. Thats why I end here.[b] I can really recommend this game to every type of gamer. It doesn´t matter if you are a casual or a competitive player.[/b]

Thanks you for reading this review. I hope you found it helpful.

This is the first negative review I’ve ever left on 'Steam', as I always try to be fair and rational when reviewing games. I’ll also be requesting a refund, which is something I never thought I’d have to do in my life. That alone should say something.

'Arc Raiders' is genuinely fun. I had a great time playing it with my friends, and the core gameplay is solid. I still want to play it even now. I have hundreds of hours in 'The Finals' and almost two hundred hours in 'Arc Raiders', so this isn’t coming from someone who barely touched the game, and wanted to hate it or the studio behind it. Unfortunately, all of that goodwill was wiped out by what happened next.

I was temporarily banned for “abnormal behavior inconsistent with normal gameplay”.
This is my first ban ever in any game. I have never used cheats, exploits, or third-party software, and my playstyle was defensive as I only engaged players who fired first. The ban happened mid-match after a brief freeze, and I was immediately kicked out. So I decided to contact support, investigate what had happened, and submit a ticket. What followed was the most frustrating part.

Customer support responses were clearly automated, which is understandable given the large player base, the issues caused by the latest and previous updates, and the growing use of artificial intelligence. Replies were sent at the same intervals from ticket creation, sometimes days apart. Other players who believed they received false bans confirmed this in a 'Discord' thread, which I will address later. I never spoke to an actual human and waited twelve days for the ticket to be "resolved". In the end, I received the same generic response everyone else gets, stating the ban was “correct” with no evidence or explanation.

There is an official thread on 'Arc Raiders (Discord)' server dedicated to false anti-cheat bans, currently sitting at 365 users, with 30+ new people joining daily and reporting the exact same issue. I understand that this may represent less than 1% of the player base, given there are around 300,000 players currently, but I believe we all deserve to be treated equally.

On top of that, community managers have been silently deleting bug report threads without any notice or explanation, which is extremely concerning and only fuels distrust in the community rather than addressing the issues.

This is not an isolated case, and it all started with 'January Update 1.11.0.' What’s even funnier is that, later in 'January Update 1.13.0.' they introduced a new ban system, which I will quote:

"A three-strikes progressive ban system is in the process of being implemented. Bans will progress from 30 days, to 60, and finally a permanent ban for repeat offenders."

If their system truly identifies cheaters, why ban them for only 30 days? Do they really trust it?

I fully understand anti-cheat systems are necessary. I also understand mistakes can happen. What’s unacceptable is that we have no transparency, proof of wrongdoing or communication.

I wanted to keep playing this game. I supported this studio for years.
But between the false ban, the artificial intelligence only customer support, and the way the situation is being handled, I no longer feel comfortable supporting 'Arc Raiders' or 'Embark Studio'.

I can’t recommend this game or risk being banned again until 'Embark' fixes the anti-cheat false positives and treats affected players like real people, since doing otherwise could harm my account or reputation.

I know that most people will not trust me and may think that I am a cheater, but believe me, these things happen more often than we realize. Until the next victim is yourself.

Great game, cautious about the future.
Extraction shooters are heavily underestimated, and this game really goes to show that. Millions still played this even months after its release. Gunplay is mostly really good, and the PvE provides lots of variety in both enemy type and difficulty. Crafting and levelling finish pretty quickly if you really have your mind set to it. I was able to max out all but one of my crafting tables about two weeks into playing, even when having a life and work. 

The game has aggression based matchmaking, which is a double-edged sword. For one, it makes it so you can easily smurf yourself into friendly lobbies and absolutely smoke a bunch of chill dudes for their loot. Meanwhile, if you went for some PvP on Stella for a few hours, you now have to spend like a day and a half running it down on free kit getting killed on sight until your aggression matchmaking finally drops you back to lobbies where you can expect to not be shot every single time by other players. It's easy to abuse, yet also hard for any players engage in combat for a little bit, encourages no one to fight in a PvPvE game, and doesn't heavily punish things like extract camping very heavily.

Bug fixes are annoyingly slow at times. To this day there is still a crafting glitch where you select how many items you want to craft, proceed to click the button to craft said items, and then the counter resets back to 1. As far as I'm aware, this has been here since day 1, and has not been patched. But don't worry, that doesn't mean they will fix arc floating through walls on Stella Montis either. The only glitch they've seemed to have patched in a really timely manner was a glitch where people phased into locked loot rooms. And they didn't actually patch it, they just made it so flamethrowers killed your character if you phased through without unlocking the door first.

Arc Buffs.
The devs have constantly talked about continuing to buff the Arc, the PvE enemies of this game. They just shadow-buffed the fireballs. Now, if you shoot them on the side on one of their rings with an Anvil or a Ferro, they won't die. Fireballs and Pops used to be one-shot-able enemies with heavy ammo weapons, in exchange for being fast moving and dangerous at close range. The arc also have 'ai learning' which as far as I'm aware, has only contributed to super annoying chaotic and unpredictable movement and sound cues for pops and fireballs. Sometimes pops will make literally no noise at all, not their beeping sounds or their movement sounds, proceed to show up right next to you, jump at you, and instantly explode, dealing 3/4 of your health if you don't have a blue shield. It also has made it so basically all flying arc, from spotters, wasps, and snitches, to rocketeers, totally not at all very obviously track on to your location, and just so happen to always """"Unintentionally"""" take a detour to drift in your direction, become aggro'd, and then start attacking you, unless you hide in cover for like an entire minute, which constantly eats up the limited time you have in each match. Embark seems to think to this day that Arc need to be buffed even more. They do not. Arc are fine. If you playtesting this game in your studio is you running around solo, with no one to pvp with, then yes, arc are manageable 98% of the time, if you're not being stupid, and not on a free kit. In a PvPvE game, Arc have become stupidly annoying. I can't tell you how many times I've been in a fight, and the game decides to spawn a pack of drones on me, or have an army of pops and fireballs decide to poke around the corner and charge at me, forcing me to duck out of cover in the middle of a battle, getting me killed. They waste ammo, sometimes heals, and announce to the entire lobby where you are, and possibly what guns you have. Not to mention Shredders on Stella Montis. Shredders are the most annoying enemy in this game. They will float around the corner and explode as soon as you walk by. Their explosions have a huge range and deal most of your health no matter what kit you have. They don't have too much health, but REQUIRE heavy ammo, otherwise you're not winning. Not to mention they're loud as hell, move super fast, and are not too uncommonly accompanied by other Arc as well, on a map that is a maze of narrow and long hallways. They seem to have no idea that buffing arc when they are (funnily enough) the most challenging part of PvP is brain dead of them. It only makes the game frustrating to play on both a casual and competitive level. Arc are fine, and didn't need to be strengthened. 

Guns
The Stitcher is a common weapon in this game, as in it is literally grey loot. Yet it's one of the most overpowered weapons in the game, especially for its worth in both materials and rarity. The Bobcat used to be the super busted SMG of this game, but they nerfed it, and now a Stitcher, a grey weapon, is as good as a Bobcat, a purple rarity weapon, that people used to grind the Locked Gate event to get the blueprint for. Most of the purple weapons besides the Vulcano are either awful, extremely situational like the Hullcracker, or just not worth the crafting materials compared to their other Blue and Green or even Grey rarity counterparts. Any shield above Green breaks down in durability super fast, which is fine, if it wasn't the only solution to not getting two tapped by an Il Toro IV, a green rarity shotgun.

Other than that, the game does have some unlucky moments here and there, like loot rarely spawning in high danger areas, or getting plopped into a lobby full of fully kitted out sweats, and the entire lobby just happens to converge on your exact location, but this is normal for extraction shooters, and just the nature of the beast, so don't allow that to make you criticize the game in ways it doesn't deserve. However, Embark seems to not have all that great of an idea as to what makes their game click, hence the bizzare rationale behind their decisions. They recently claimed that spawning in halfway through a match (which is 30 minutes long, meaning you have 15 minutes left) actually gets you more loot! It doesn't. This is a lie, they just don't want you hammering them for not having every match be a fresh match, as this would hurt queue times, and they don't wanna be known as the company that made a game with long queue times. Along with them not patching glitches, having really poor balancing for weapons, and more, is why I am not so sure about how this game will fair in the future, especially with Marathon just around the corner. They have the chance to really drop the ball and lose out to a competitor, even though that competitor is facing their own issues atm.

Embark also recently has shown a history of shadow nerfing and buffing things. I hate this. Please for the love of god, tell me ALL of what changed about the game I paid money for, and dedicate hours of my weekly life to. 

Cosmetics in this game are also pretty bad. They're definitely going for a retro futuristic "scrappy" kind of look. Not so much like Rust, but more like 'high tech stitched together with duct tape'. The problem is that following this makes most cosmetics look kinda meh, especially the ones they expect you to pay money for. 

Overall it's a great game that's struggling to be excellent, and might shot itself in the foot in the next few months. You're definitely missing out by not playing, but don't be too terribly surprised if your friends stop playing by March or April of this year. If I were you, buy it now and have fun, but it's now or never. I'd say this game has a 50/50 shot of shitting the bed and falling off

Rust markets itself as a “survival game.” That’s a lie. Rust is a full-time job where your salary is trauma and your boss is a 14-year-old with a shotgun and a racial slur ready to deploy at 3am.

You spawn naked on a beach, optimistic. Ten minutes later you’re dead, looted, and questioning your self-worth because someone named xXCLANLEADER69Xx beat you to death with a rock while screaming into a £300 mic. This cycle repeats until optimism is fully removed from your personality.

Progress in Rust is measured not in fun, but in hours lost to paranoia. You will wake up in the night to “check the base.” You will cancel plans because “the wipe just started.” You will defend this decision to loved ones who are already planning interventions.

Every base you build is temporary. Every friendship is fake. Every door code will be betrayed. Rust teaches powerful life lessons like:
• Trust no one
• Sleep is optional
• Your time means nothing

The game excels at giving you hope just long enough to hurt you more. You farm for six hours, log off for ten minutes, and come back to ashes. No note. No mercy. Just silence and the distant sound of someone recycling your stuff.

And yet… you’ll reinstall it. Every time. Because once in a while, you win a fight. Once in a while, the sun hits your base just right. Once in a while, you feel something again.

Rust doesn’t respect you. It doesn’t care about balance. It doesn’t care about your life.
But you’ll keep playing. Because Rust isn’t entertainment.

It’s Stockholm Syndrome with crafting.

Would I recommend it?
Absolutely not.

See you after wipe.

Rust is one of the most exciting and unpredictable survival games I’ve played. The core gameplay—gathering resources, crafting gear, building a base, and defending what’s yours—always keeps you on your toes. I love how every server feels like its own little world full of danger, tension, and opportunity.

The sense of progression feels great: you start with almost nothing, and before you know it you’ve built a fortified compound and are running around with high-end weapons. The PvP is intense and nerve-racking in the best way, and even when you lose everything it’s strangely fun to scramble back and life begins again.

What really makes Rust fun for me is the player interactions—whether it’s teaming up, ambushing someone, trading goods, or forming alliances, every play session creates its own stories and memories. The building system is versatile, and although the graphics aren’t flashy, they fit the gritty atmosphere perfectly.

Sure, it can be tough and sometimes frustrating (especially when raided), but that’s part of what makes it memorable. If you’re into open-ended survival where anything can happen, Rust is a blast.

👍 Pros

Wild, emergent gameplay with real player drama

Deep crafting and base building

Great sense of achievement and progression

Tons of replay value

👎 Cons

Can feel harsh or chaotic for new players

Loss of gear can be discouraging at times

Overall, Rust is incredibly fun and keeps me coming back for more. Highly recommended if you like survival games with freedom, challenge, and unpredictable moments!

《Rust：在残酷世界中学习生存与人性》

大家好，
今天我想向大家介绍一款非常有特色的生存类游戏——《Rust》。

《Rust》是一款开放世界多人在线生存游戏。玩家进入游戏时几乎一无所有，没有武器、没有资源，甚至连衣服都没有。在这个世界里，你需要通过采集资源、制作工具、建造基地，努力活下来。

但《Rust》真正独特的地方，并不仅仅是“生存”本身，而是人与人之间的关系。在游戏中，其他玩家既可能是你的盟友，也可能是你的敌人。你可以选择合作，一起建设、分享资源；也可以选择对抗，抢夺物资，甚至背叛曾经的朋友。

正因为这种高度自由的互动，《Rust》被称为“最真实的人性实验室”。在这里，信任非常珍贵，但也非常脆弱。一次错误的判断，可能就会让你失去辛苦积累的一切。

同时，《Rust》也强调策略与耐心。玩家需要合理规划时间，选择何时冒险、何时隐藏自己。建造基地不仅要考虑防御，还要考虑位置、资源和其他玩家的威胁。

当然，《Rust》并不是一款轻松的游戏。它节奏紧张，失败成本高，有时甚至让人感到挫败。但正是这种残酷，让每一次成功都显得格外有价值。

总的来说，《Rust》不仅是一款游戏，更是一种体验。它让我们思考：在资源有限、规则最少的世界中，我们会选择合作，还是对抗？我们会坚持道德，还是只追求生存？

谢谢大家！

I woke up in a forest with no memories, no clothes, and a rock that felt suspiciously judgmental. The sun was rising, birds were chirping, and for one tiny moment I thought, “This might be peaceful.”

That’s when I heard footsteps.

Three men appeared between the trees like a low-budget boss fight. They were wearing armor made of metal and confidence. One of them was screaming into his mic for no reason. Another was crouching repeatedly, like his knees were on a timer.

They circled me.

“Don’t move,” one said, while moving aggressively.
“Why you built like that,” said another, who looked like a refrigerator with legs.
The third just stared. That was the worst one.

I tried to run. I ran directly into a bear. The bear respected the men more than me.

They took my rock. They took my torch. One of them made me punch a tree while they argued about who would get my bones. I didn’t even know I had bones yet.

Eventually they got bored and told me I was “free.” I took two steps. Gunshot. Darkness.

I woke up again on the beach. Different spot. Same life. I built a base this time. Four walls, a door, dreams. I felt unstoppable.

While I was crafting a sleeping bag, someone played loud music through my wall. Then the wall exploded. Then my dreams exploded. A man ran through my base, looked at my empty boxes, shook his head in disappointment, and left.

Later that night, I sat by a campfire, alone, staring into the flames, when a stranger walked up, dropped me food, nodded, and vanished into the darkness like a forest cryptid.

Ten minutes later, that same guy raided me.

I learned something that day.

I’ve owned every FIFA game from ’97 to ’21. After stepping away from consoles for a few years, I built a PC and picked up FC26.

I was expecting a much bigger leap from FIFA 21. Mechanically, it still feels almost identical — and honestly, even FIFA 21 didn’t feel that different from 18 or 19. The core gameplay hasn’t really evolved in any meaningful way.

Manager Mode is in the same boat. There are a few tweaks here and there, but nothing that fundamentally changes how it plays. It still feels like the same mode I’ve been playing for years, just with some new menus and minor adjustments.

The graphics are definitely nicer, but even that jump wasn’t as dramatic as I expected going from FIFA 21 on an old Xbox to FC26 on a high‑end gaming PC.

Summary:
In the end, even though so much of it feels familiar, I still find myself recommending FC26. The gameplay is smooth, the matches are genuinely fun, and there’s an undeniable charm to the formula—even if it hasn’t changed much in years. Sure, the focus has clearly shifted toward Ultimate Team lately, mostly for financial reasons, but there’s still plenty of enjoyment to be had outside of that mode. If you’re coming back after a break or just want a solid football game to sink time into, it still delivers where it counts.

There is sadly no competition on the football game market.

FC 26 – 3/10 – Fun Game, But Unplayable on Steam Due to Constant Crashes

FC 26 had all the makings of a solid, fun football game. The gameplay is engaging, with fluid mechanics and a satisfying level of control over your team. The matches are intense, the player movements are smooth, and the action feels just right when it works. For a moment, it seems like the perfect pick for casual football fans or those looking for a quick but enjoyable gaming experience. Unfortunately, that's where the praise ends—because the game simply doesn’t work properly on Steam.

The major issue with FC 26 is its stability. Despite the fun gameplay on offer, the game crashes frequently, making it nearly impossible to get through a full match or enjoy any extended sessions. Whether it's a random freeze mid-game, crashing to the desktop after loading a match, or losing progress after an unexpected shutdown, the game’s technical issues ruin what could have been an otherwise enjoyable experience. At this point, FC 26 feels like it’s been released in an unfinished state on Steam, with no clear fixes in sight.

When it does work, the game is fun. The mechanics are solid, the visuals are decent (if not groundbreaking), and the sound design—while nothing special—provides a good atmosphere during matches. There’s a satisfying sense of progression, team management, and strategy that could keep you invested for hours. If the game ran smoothly, it’d be a decent football sim. However, these positives are completely overshadowed by the constant crashes that prevent any meaningful progress.

The fact that FC 26 is unplayable on Steam is a huge issue, and it’s disappointing because the game has potential. For players who are able to get through a match without it crashing, there’s a solid experience waiting for them, but that’s a big “if.” The lack of a reliable experience on such a major platform makes it hard to recommend.

If you’re still determined to play it, I highly suggest buying it through the EA App instead. It seems to be more stable there, and you’ll actually be able to enjoy the game without the constant crashing and frustration that comes with the Steam version.

FC 26 3/10 – A Fun Game, If You Can Actually Play It
FC 26 could have been a solid sports title, but the constant crashing makes it unplayable for most players on Steam. The potential is there, but it’s buried under a mountain of technical issues. Until the developers address the stability problems, this game is more frustrating than fun. If you're looking for a working football game, you’re better off buying it on the EA App, where the experience is at least more reliable.

How does a game released in 2026 still run like it’s poorly optimized early access trash?
What really pisses me off is where the effort clearly went. Ultimate Team is shoved in your face like a slot machine. Packs, promos, shiny cards nonstop. Meanwhile Career Mode feels ignored, Pro Clubs barely works, and anything that doesn’t make money gets treated like it doesn’t matter. It’s obvious the devs aren’t trying to make a better football game anymore they’re just trying to squeeze wallets.
At this point EA Sports isn’t even hiding it. Full price game, bugs everywhere, performance issues, then microtransactions on top like we should be grateful. Fixes come late, if at all, and every patch somehow breaks something else. It honestly feels like they know people will buy it anyway, so why bother?
This isn’t a “bad launch” or “minor issues.” This is the same problems every year, and they choose not to fix them because fixing them doesn’t sell packs. Simple as that.

I didn’t expect perfection. I just wanted a football game that runs properly and feels fair. Instead I got stutters, scripting, greed, and the same recycled nonsense wrapped in hype.

If you skipped last year’s FIFA, congrats — you already played this one.
If you’re thinking of buying it, don’t. Seriously. Save your money.

I grew up dreaming of owning a FIFA game. Back then, money was tight, and the idea of finally playing it felt like a milestone. Fast forward to today, I finally own it—and the experience has been nothing short of disappointing.
Performance Issues
- FPS drops: The game frequently dips to single-digit frames, making matches feel unplayable.
- Controller delay: Inputs lag, leaving me frustrated as players fail to respond in crucial moments.
- Gameplay stutters: Sometimes, players just stop moving mid-game, breaking immersion completely.
Server & Optimization
It’s not just me—many players online report the same problems. EA’s servers feel unreliable, and the game itself is poorly optimized. For a title that costs so much, this level of instability is unacceptable.
Final Verdict
Owning FIFA was once a dream. Playing it has turned into a nightmare. Between the broken servers, unresponsive gameplay, and lack of optimization, this is the last FIFA/EA FC title I’ll ever buy. It’s simply not worth the money—or the sanity it drains.

Having played FIFA games since FIFA 13, I'll admit the gameplay does take some getting used to. I was initially appalled at the how clumsy and unresponsive the players felt, but IMO it's more realistic after getting used to the game. Additionally, I will give credit to some of the details of Manager Mode and Player Career Mode. 
However, this is one of the least optimized games I have ever played. The number of random disconnects, server timeouts, and random bugs I encounter in this game would make me believe this was an early access beta. The animations are poor, as evidenced by watching some goal instant replays and seeing collision physics poorly integrated with balls going through people's legs and body parts morphing together. It's a true shame how inconsistent it really is. 
Furthermore, having played mostly Player Career mode in every FIFA game I played, I can say this is an extremely disappointing showing from EA FC 26. Going back to FIFA 17 and seeing how much effort they put into The Journey, allowing you to truly immerse yourself into a story was fantastic. It's saddening to see their pure focus on Ultimate Team and the lack of effort that results in other gameplay modes. 
Finally, it's just too easy to progress both in UT and Career Mode. In previous games, you would start UT with a bronze squad and celebrate when you finally could afford your first gold player. An 80 rated squad was something that took genuine effort, where now you are gifted 90 OVR players from the moment you start the game. In Player Career, you used to start out as a 65 OVR and be sent on loan to third division teams to prove your worth. You would have to genuinely grind and immerse yourself in the game to succeed, and now none of that exists. 
Overall, its fun to play as an arcade game, but as the number one Football video game on the market, it is extremely flawed.

Its crazy that with the better technology and internet we have available today, the game feels worse, more annoying, and less satisfying to play than in did 10 years ago. The Enhanced Edition looks genuinely impressive in 4K with ray tracing set to Ultra, even while using DLSS. I’m running an RTX 5070 12 GB, and loading into Los Santos still feels like a treat—driving around, stealing cars, and just taking in the detail never really gets old.

I’m about 40% through the campaign on my first full playthrough. I originally bought the game as a benchmark title while I was still on an RTX 3060 Ti, and at some point it upgraded me to the Enhanced Edition. From what I’ve seen, the Legacy versions still work best if you’re deep into LSPDFR modding, but I had no trouble using trainer menus for cheats, spawning vehicles, and stress-testing the game. That alone gave me hours of entertainment.

The story held my interest up until Trevor entered the picture. At this point in my life, I find parts of the narrative excessive and overly graphic, especially for younger players. That’s just my perspective as a 46-year-old gamer, and it doesn’t diminish what the game does well mechanically.

Where GTA V still shines is in its systems, world detail, and sheer flexibility—especially on PC. Between mods, FiveM, and the overall sandbox design, it’s easy to recommend this to PC players coming from GTA IV or older console versions. I’m averaging around 180 FPS on Ultra with ray tracing enabled and DLSS set to Quality, and that performance alone makes the experience feel fresh all over again.
