⭐ [b]RECOMMENDED[/b] ⭐

== Visuals / Ray-Traced Reflections ==
The biggest upgrade in GTA V Enhanced is the ray-traced reflections. The city looks much better, especially when the road is wet. Puddles reflect lights clearly, cars look shiny, and glass buildings reflect the environment. At night, the reflections make the city feel more realistic. Close to Cyberpunk 2077 level of realism, but not quite. For screenshots, this is really good.

== Familiar but Improved ==
The game still feels familiar, but the visual upgrade makes it feel fresh again. The improvements are not too much, but they are very noticeable. Everything looks cleaner and more detailed.

== Loading ==
Loading is faster than before. You won't age 5 years before you can play the game.

== Performance ==
If your PC can run it, turning on ray tracing is worth it. The visual quality is much better and makes the experience more enjoyable.

== Final Thoughts ==
This version makes the game feel like a whole mood. Driving around without doing anything already feels good.

Summary:
Great reflections, strong atmosphere, very good vibes.

In an era of gaming dominated by high-stress battle royales, predatory microtransactions, and hyper-realistic graphics, Stardew Valley stands apart as a breath of fresh country air. What begins as a simple farming simulator quickly reveals itself to be a profound, therapeutic, and deeply engaging experience that feels less like playing a game and more like coming home.

The "Just One More Day" Phenomenon
The premise is a classic trope: you inherit your grandfather's old farm plot to escape the soul-crushing drudgery of a corporate office job. However, the execution is flawless. The core gameplay loop—clearing land, planting seeds, watering crops, and harvesting the fruits of your labor—is incredibly satisfying.
There is a unique rhythm to the game that hooks you immediately. You wake up, check the weather, tend to your animals, and then decide how to spend your energy. Do you want to brave the depths of the mines to find rare ores? Do you want to spend a lazy afternoon fishing at the beach? or do you want to forage in the secret woods?

 Note: The genius of Stardew Valley is the lack of punishment. If you miss a harvest or forget to talk to a villager, the game doesn't punish you. It waits for you. This creates a stress-free environment that is purely motivated by your own desire to improve your farm.

A Living, Breathing World
Visually, the game is a triumph of 16-bit pixel art. The changing of the seasons is not just a gameplay mechanic but an aesthetic shift that changes the entire mood of the valley. From the floating pink petals of Spring to the cozy, melancholic snow of Winter, every screen is a painting.

Accompanying these visuals is a soundtrack that can only be described as iconic. Composed by the game's sole creator, Eric Barone (ConcernedApe), the music perfectly encapsulates the feeling of the season. The upbeat tunes of Summer make you want to work, while the gentle piano melodies of Winter encourage introspection.

Heart and Soul
Perhaps the most surprising depth lies in the villagers of Pelican Town. At first glance, they appear to be archetypes: the jock, the prep, the grumpy old man. But as you build relationships with them through gifts and conversation, you uncover genuine human struggles. You help characters deal with depression, alcoholism, PTSD, and family abandonment. The writing is empathetic and real, making the town feel populated by friends rather than NPCs.

The Verdict
Stardew Valley is a labor of love that respects the player’s time and intelligence. It is a game about connections—connecting with nature, connecting with a community, and reconnecting with a sense of peace that is often lost in modern life.

Whether you are a hardcore gamer looking for efficiency and optimization, or a casual player looking for a cozy escape, this game has something for you. It is, quite simply, pixelated perfection.
Score: 10/10

Path of Exile 2 feels like an ARPG made by people who actually hate boredom. Even in its current state, it already has more depth than most finished games. If you played the first Path of Exile, this feels familiar—but meaner, prettier, and way more demanding.

The campaign caught me off guard. I expected a chill run to endgame and instead got repeatedly humbled by bosses that forced me to actually think. Every roadblock sent me straight to my gear, skills, and resistances like I was debugging my own build. Change something, try again, die less, repeat.

The constant build tweaking is where the addiction kicks in. Your character never feels “done,” and when something finally clicks, it feels insanely rewarding. It’s challenging, punishing, and fun in that “I hate this but I love it” way.

Path of Exile 2 – A Masterclass in How to Waste Your Time

Path of Exile 2 is a stunning reminder that no matter how good your trailers look, you can still ship a complete mess. This game feels less like a sequel and more like a public beta duct-taped to a marketing campaign.

Let’s start with the exploit disaster. Watching the whole Fubgun situation unfold was embarrassing. An exploit runs wild, certain players benefit massively, the economy gets warped, and the response feels slow, inconsistent, and half-hearted. Whether you exploited or not, the damage was already done. Nothing screams “competitive integrity” like letting broken mechanics exist long enough for people to get rich off them before quietly sweeping it under the rug.

Now onto the servers, which are somehow worse than the balance. Constant disconnects. Infinite loading screens. “Failed to connect to server” over and over again like it’s a core gameplay mechanic. Nothing kills hype faster than sitting at a loading screen wondering if you’re about to play the game or just get booted back to the login screen—for the fifth time in ten minutes.

And when you do connect? Enjoy rubber-banding, instance failures, and random desync like it’s 2013. For a modern ARPG that’s supposed to compete at the top of the genre, this is straight up unacceptable.

The worst part is that PoE 2 could be great. The bones are there. But instead of feeling polished, it feels rushed, unstable, and disrespectful of players’ time. Between exploit scandals, server instability, and endless connection issues, the game constantly fights you instead of letting you have fun.

Right now, PoE 2 isn’t a next-gen ARPG.
It’s a stress test with loot.

Final verdict:
Amazing potential buried under bad decisions, broken systems, and servers held together by hopes and prayers. Come back in 5 years—maybe it’ll be finished by then.

Let me start off by saying, between Steam and my Nintendo Switch, I have over 2000 hours invested in this game and have been in this community for quite a while.

I'll start off with some of the positives by saying that this game can be fun, when you get lucky enough to get in a good lobby. The crossovers are cool and their original characters are pretty neat, too, so you have a variety of characters to choose from and you can dress them up all cool and stuff, too. The game has relatively consistent updates and quite a few events throughout the year, including some limited-time game modes to spice things up, which are pretty fun. Some of them are even more fun than the default game mode.

Now onto the bad stuff... Killer queue times are absolute ass. You will be sitting in lobbies for AGES just to get into a single match. Survivor queue times aren't as bad, thankfully. Secondly, this game is not beginner friendly at all in terms of it's players and basically everything about how THE GAME ITSELF is. I'll start off with the players; the player base has a HUGE aggression problem and is generally unwelcoming towards new players, so if you're trying to figure out how the game works in a public lobby, then prepare for hostility from other players. Hell, even if you aren't a new player, lobbies have issues with griefing and, best of all, harassment in endgame chat. Lovely. As for the game itself not being beginner friendly, it is a CONSTANT learning curve because of how much there is in the game. There are 48 survivors, each with three perks they come with, and there are 38 killers, also with three unique perks they come with AND the killers come with special built-in abilities. There are also general killer/survivor perks. You can probably do some of the math on that. I bring this up to say that there is so much stuff to keep tabs on what it does that any newcomer would be overwhelmed by it. This isn't to say the variety is a BAD thing, but it's just reasonably confusing to anyone trying to start the game. This is made worse by the SUPER out of date tutorial. The tutorial teaches you very basic shit, but there is NOTHING to tell you about perks and items in said tutorial. 

Now, onto the bigger and way more disappointing issue... The devs themselves are incompetent. There is a lack of proper care taken when it comes to listening to the community... And by that I mean they hardly seem to listen to community issues at all, unless it has to do with cosmetic contests and what crossovers people may want, and even then, they often fuck those up, too. There has been such a MASSIVE amount of bugs over the years that have affected the quality of the game. Sure, bugs are bound to happen, but when you do public test build runs before chapter releases and have the community make you aware of massive issues, only to ignore them and release the new update without doing a proper bug fix anyways, it's not just a "bugs happen" type of issue, it's a "the developers do not care enough about their product" sort of issue. How does a game live on? Originally starting out as a serious co-op horror experience, Dead by Daylight has morphed into an arcade game rife with pop culture characters and needless tweaks. A question posed by many players is, "Does it work?" And the answer is: sometimes.
    If one were to look back on Dead by Daylight's humble origins, they could see a game brimming with potential. A limited array of characters and a highly addictive game-loop gave DbD a leg-up in comparison to its multiplayer competition--even trumping the asymmetrical-horror competition that would later follow as a result. The game ran on atmosphere and depended on you (the player) being terrified or being terrifying. Many would say this was the 'golden-age' of the game (and it was good), but to say that is to disregard the improvements made by the modern DbD.
    Dead by Daylight might not be terrifying anymore--or at the least, not in the intended way--but still it survives. But how? The 'game-ification' of DbD has vastly improved (or made engaging) the previously barebones gameplay loop. What was once a cast of a measly three killers has now expanded far into the double digits.  Both the survivors and killers have benefitted from licenses concerning some of the biggest names in horror and each game is now a true surprise in terms of what killer you'll face. Additionally, the game's weakened focus on horror but instead on engagement creates matches that feel more fun to play in succession. Balancing issues aside, games are usually a tense toss-up of abilities. However, these aforementioned balancing issues and the lack of focus on horror (among other aspects of the game) fail to connect with many players, and rightfully so. Newly added killers are usually nerfed into oblivion following their release and following dominance in matches, and new survivors are usually only justified by their licensing and expensive skins, hardly ever having decent or fun perks. Such is the consequence of bloating the game's perk pool and character slots beyond what was once thought possible in the early epochs of the game's existence. Yet, DbD has survived even when many other games of its kind have died. And that's because it refuses to stay still. The game is constantly evolving: both to its benefit and detriment.
   So, again: how does a game live? In the case of DbD, the answer is momentum. Pure inertia. There have been multiple moments when the game has almost faltered and faded into obscurity, but whether Behavior Interactive actually balances the game's prominent issues or just piles on another broken DLC, people still tune in to see how it's holding up: which is by a shoestring. But still, it holds. All in all, DbD is certainly adequate, but only time will tell if it stays that way.

Or what they won't show is that the team may have been friends on coms who didn't care to do objectives and only wanted to troll until their inevitable demise. --------- The developers use player match data to ASSUME people are playing the game the way it's intended and then use that data to mess things up in serious matches.

I’ve spent over two thousand hours in Dead by Daylight, and this is one of those cases where the number isn’t there to flex, but to make one thing clear: I know what I’m talking about. I started playing in 2017, and even before that, back in 2016, I was already following the game closely — watching streams, reading forums, trying to understand where it was heading. Back then, it was genuinely a unique project. Dead by Daylight was a horror game, not an attraction. Tension was constant, every sound mattered, every mistake was punished, but every correct decision gave you a real sense of control and satisfaction.

A killer could wipe the entire lobby if they played well, if they thought ahead, if they knew how to read the map and the players. At the same time, a single truly skilled survivor could loop the killer long enough for the team to calmly finish three, four, sometimes even five generators. Not because the killer was weak, but because the survivor understood timings, positioning, how to run loops properly, and didn’t panic. It wasn’t chaotic running — it was deliberate gameplay, where your individual skill genuinely mattered. That honest exchange of skill is what kept the game alive.

Very little of that remains today. Dead by Daylight has stopped being a horror game and has turned into a mass-market live service. Behaviour deliberately chose the path of simplification and monetization. Instead of atmosphere and fear, we get skins. Instead of tension, we get endless killers and survivors from movies and TV shows. Instead of proper balance, we get constant buffs designed to make new content sell better. From a business perspective, this might be a success, but from a gameplay perspective, it’s a slow and steady killing of the original idea.

Playing killer today is laughably easy. You can be an average player, you don’t even have to think that much, and you’ll still consistently get 4Ks. The game forgives mistakes, the mechanics actively push you toward winning, and most killers don’t require serious mindgames or planning anymore. And yet there are still people who somehow struggle to win as killer, and honestly, I don’t understand what you have to do wrong to lose under the current conditions.

On the other side, survivor gameplay has become a parody of itself. It’s no longer survival or horror — it’s endless running in circles with constant downs. Even if you’re a skilled survivor, your individual skill barely matters anymore. Maps feel like they were deliberately designed without proper safe structures, and you go down every thirty to forty seconds simply because there’s nowhere left to play. Add killers’ bloodlust, their constantly buffed abilities, and what you end up with isn’t gameplay, but a mess where skill isn’t rewarded — it’s devalued. Skill checks stopped being a challenge a long time ago; they’re just a mechanical rhythm-game action that does nothing to compensate for the overall imbalance.

The worst part of all this is the lack of real competition. Dead by Daylight is effectively a monopoly in its genre, and Behaviour knows it. When there are no real alternatives, developers don’t have to listen to their players. They can keep adding more paid content, dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and call it “development.” Paid characters often come with strong perks, and even if this isn’t pay-to-win on paper, in practice you’re either paying with money or paying with your time and nerves.

The latest Stranger Things Chapter 2 update was the final confirmation of where this game is heading for me. They released an extremely overpowered killer, completely unbalanced, against whom survivors can do almost nothing. And the funniest part is that the studio had several weeks for testing and polishing, but instead they chose the familiar strategy: release a broken character, cash in on sales because people will buy it after getting destroyed in a few matches, and only then — maybe, someday — nerf it. It feels cynical and kills any remaining trust.

Dead by Daylight was my favorite game for many years. I defended it, recommended it to friends, and justified the developers’ decisions. But over the past few years, Behaviour has been systematically turning it into a soulless monetized product. This isn’t evolution or growth — it’s degradation. That’s why I can’t recommend this game for purchase. If you still decide to get into it, be aware that you’re signing up for dozens of DLCs, hundreds of skins, and a constant feeling that the game is deliberately pushing you to spend more money and more time. It’s a sad example of how a company, chasing profit, is willing to completely kill an idea that was once truly unique.

I have really enjoyed my time with BF6, it's a bit different to previous Battlefield titles but it is engaging and fun. 
I don't know if this is a problem in every multiplayer genre now or if it's just my experience here, but it just feels like the people who do play this game refuse to create a community, I rarely hear anyone talk in voice chat, when people do talk in text chat another person usually tells them to shut up. The forums/Reddit for the game are full of complaints about things that don't actually feel like issues to someone who has played for a couple hundred hours now. 

I don't know. Most of my friends who I did squad up with have moved on to other titles, without actually buying this game or the previous entry(s), and the current community just isn't very friendly or tight knit.

We have the ability to host our own servers completely for free with just a few clicks, and you can go onto the portal website and customise everything from movement sliding to health to individual weapon bans, But nobody does it - the reddit and forum constantly complain about a lack of a server browser or matchmaking issues but nobody makes a server and goes "Hey I'm hosting an official conquest rotation, join on ABCXYZ code this weekend". And even if someone did, nobody replies or joins in positively.

Are gaming clans and groups just not a thing anymore? I don't know.

There is a lot of fun to be had here, and I've only played the multiplayer. Creatives have the full Portal SDK to play with. 

Singleplayer was dissapointing after BFBC, BF3, and BF1/V stories. They really phoned it in. Which is a shame because honestly they don't even need to have a COD cinematic campaign like those games. They could just have multiplayer style map scenarios where you fight through things that build the world as it would have been envisioned. A beach landing, an extraction mission, an MCOM defusal, short text stories or cutscenes explaining what you're being dropped into or why you're fighting in this universe. Shrug.
Maps are incredibly small for battlefield, no one asked for redsec, hit registration is awful. Can't justify the price point in it's current state.

This game was designed by the MBAs and not by the artists/game devs. There are so many design elements that are clearly there just to artificially boost their "metrics" at the expense of the end user experience. They made the maps tiny so that you were constantly forced to fight and there is no downtime to recover/plan, and no space for big flanks or vehicle play. The end result is a meat-grinder where you run in, maybe get a few kills, and die over and over. 

Most guns have a ridiculously fast time to kill (several are sub 200 ms at close range, meaning it is physically impossible to react if you start getting shot. And the maps are tiny, so 60-80% of the engagements are within 30 meters. See the problem? This plus the really twitchy movement they copied over from 2042 is seriously so exhausting. I find myself burning out and getting frustrated after about 2-4 rounds at most. There weren't that many maps at launch in the first place, and at least half of them are borderline unplayable, so I end up queueing for just the same 4 or 5 maps every game, which contributes to the burnout.

I will keep playing this game (mostly because there is just not a great alternative for this "all about battle" genre that Battlefield used to be) and hope content drops in future seasons will ameliorate some of the problems. But I think there are core design philosophy issues that won't be solved by just throwing more stuff at the problem. Maybe could pull a 2042 where they went back and overhauled every single map and resolved a ton of the pain points. I doubt EA will see that as providing enough short-term gain though, so I'm not optimistic.

Conclusion: I wish I had waited a year on this for them to flesh out content, listen to player feedback, and iron out glaring technical issues (which I didn't even get into here as this is already getting long).

Battlefield 6 felt like a step in the right direction to recapture the gameplay and feeling of some of the best entries in the series. The gameplay isn't perfect - maps could be larger, vehicle roles can feel a little underwhelming, and the pace of the game surely isn't BF2, but it was just FUN.

The problem is that the game is now completely unplayable for me. Attempting to launch the game results in endless Javelin errors and hang-ups. Every new session requires verifying game files, attempting to reinstall or repair Javelin, and reboots. Occasionally the game will launch, but unfortunately it doesn't last; there are frequent crashes with no warning or error message. Sometimes there will be one related to DirectX with no viable solution. 

I don't know what happened to this game, but it is literally unplayable now. Buyer beware, you might end up with a $70 boat anchor in your Steam library. It's a shame, because I'd love to be able to play again.

No.

1) it was in the previous games

There are a few slight issues with the game, the main one for me being the lack of very large maps that Battlefield veterans were possibly expecting, however this could change with time as new maps are released.

This game unfortunately has Seasons AND a cash shop but it is all cosmetic items only. Therefore it has unlockable and purchasable skins for weapons, vehicles and soldiers which is both a good and a bad thing. The majority of skins are tasteful and fine, however some do stand out slightly as looking out of place in a Battlefield game, but nothing like the nonsense that is present on Call of Duty these days. I found Season 1 very grindy and just when you think you’ve finished it all they release another tier of the battlepass.

My only other gripe with the game would be that crossplay is enabled by default with no way to turn it off in-game. You have to edit an .ini file to disable crossplay. With crossplay disabled it does take a long time to find games sometimes, so for that reason I leave it enabled. I find console players really let you down generally in this game, with behaviour such as not reviving team mates, not playing the objective, not using transport vehicles correctly and abandoning team mates at spawn and so on. They can really turn the tide of battle and can cause your team to loose more often than win.

With a large number of weapons and gadgets available to suit your play style the devs have done a good job with weapon feel, bullet drop etc. Some complained of hit registration issues, but this is not something I have had a problem with at all in 100+ hours.

Looking forward to seeing how this game evolves over time, hopefully cosmetics stay true to the look and feel of a Battlefield title.

BF6 draws you in with classic battlefield expectations. You explore the maps, classes, and weapons until you settle in to a few favorites, because nobody has time to invest into unlocking all the attachments for a variety of weapons. With the number of vehicles and their impact, I find it rarely makes sense to play anything but engineer. SMGs also seem to be the most consistent and provide great short to mid range options. After getting bored of it, I switched to recon. The mini scout is the way to go and is significantly easier to make short to mid ranged hits with. Its easy to control an obj from a short distance with a little positioning and skill. The problem is, with limited maps, you end up doing the same thing each map. You know this is the best route, the best sniping spot, that the enemy will helicopter to F to take it so you need to protect it, etc. With all the chaos and variety, it becomes a game of simple, repeating options unless you voluntarily choose todo something unique, like waste your time on assault class.

That being said, they do have a few large maps with combined arms (Jets, Tanks, Transport vehicles, etc) and the gameplay there is amazing. The gun feedback and gameplay essentials are there - they just need more large maps and the game will become S-Tier.

Battlefield 6 is a hollow shell of its former self, trading the franchise’s iconic scale for a frantic, identity-less experience that feels more like a Call of Duty clone than a true tactical shooter. The lack of content at launch is staggering; with a pathetic selection of weapons and gadgets, you'll feel like you’ve seen everything the game has to offer within the first few hours. This emptiness is exacerbated by a transparently greedy leveling system that turns basic progression into a soul-crushing grind, clearly designed to frustrate players into purchasing XP boosters rather than rewarding genuine skill or playtime.

The map design is arguably the biggest disappointment, as DICE has abandoned the "All-Out Warfare" philosophy for cramped, tiny arenas that offer zero room for strategic maneuvering. Half of the maps in the rotation are absolute garbage, lacking any coherent flow and resulting in a constant, mindless meat grinder. By shrinking the play space and cranking up the movement speed to mimic its competitors, Battlefield has sacrificed its soul. It has replaced the deliberate, squad-based tension of previous entries with a twitchy, individualistic gameplay loop that makes vehicles feel irrelevant and tactics feel obsolete.

[h1]Disappointing — especially for solo players[/h1]


[h3]Portal Without Real Freedom[/h3]

Disappointing experience overall. Despite promising Portal trailers Battlefield 6 [b]no longer allows true solo vs. bots or proper small-scale co-op[/b], which was the main reason I bought it. Had this been clear before release, I would not have purchased the game, even at a discount!

[h3]The PvP is more than okay[/h3]

As a player of the series since Battlefield 2, I find the PvP quite solid, even if it is unfortunately less classic than expected and instead adopts a Call of Duty–like pace. This is disappointing and does not fully meet the advertising promise. The sound design and graphics, by contrast, are outstanding.

[h3]For the US of A![/h3]

Turning to the campaign, the story appears engaging at first but becomes increasingly absurd as it unfolds. The PvP gameplay mechanics are nevertheless integrated very effectively. The AI companions, however, seem to have skipped basic training: they constantly rush ahead, engage enemies with long-range rifles from 20 cm distance, then retreat toward the player—often stepping directly into the line of sight and blocking the view of enemies firing at their backs from behind. The result is a complete lack of immersion and considerable frustration. Even the supposedly “cool” voice lines fail to compensate.

[h3]Search and destroy — but mainly search, search, search[/h3]

The game menu, incidentally, appears to have been designed and implemented by a UX/UI intern who, at least in my estimation, suffers from any serious orientation disorder. The menu is a maze with a steep learning curve. The sole redeeming feature is the menu soundtrack, which was likely not that intern’s responsibility. ;-)

I have spent over 100 hours with Battlefield 6 across three separate uninstall and reinstall cycles, including getting a refund at launch, which means one of two things. Either I love it, or I am trapped in a complicated situationship with it and refuse to admit it is unhealthy.

On paper, Battlefield 6 is everything I asked for. Big maps, shiny explosions, helicopters doing things helicopters probably should not be doing, and that classic Battlefield promise that teamwork matters. In practice, teamwork is more of a light suggestion, like the speed limit or a warning label.

The gunplay feels fantastic when the servers agree with you. When they do not, it feels like your bullets are being politely negotiated away by the netcode. Hit registration can be rock solid one match and purely conceptual the next. Time to kill swings wildly between “tactical shooter” and “blink and you are dead”, often within the same firefight. It keeps you alert, mostly because you never know which version you are getting.

The maps are huge, beautiful, and occasionally so empty that you start questioning your life choices while jogging towards the objective. When the action clicks, it is glorious chaos. When it does not, you are being farmed by a jet you never saw while your squad mate is 600 metres away trying to snipe someone who moved on emotionally five minutes ago.

Balance changes arrive regularly and with great confidence. Sometimes they fix things. Sometimes they introduce exciting new problems. Specialists remain a bold design choice that not everyone asked for but everyone now has very strong opinions about. Vehicle balance still feels like it was discussed briefly and then committed to out of spite.

Performance and bugs have improved since launch, to be fair. The game now mostly works as intended, which is a low bar but one Battlefield has historically enjoyed limbo dancing under. Cheaters exist, patches break things, and every update is an adventure you did not consent to but are somehow still excited for.

For context, my longest recon kill is 851 metres (check profile if you don't believe ;). This is not a humblebrag, it is a cry for help. Because despite this, my squad mates still cannot seem to spot enemies, revive teammates, or understand that the objective is not optional side content.

Do I recommend it? Yes. In the same way you recommend a rollercoaster that occasionally throws you into a wall. It is loud, messy, ridiculous, frustrating, and when it is good, it is very, very good. Battlefield 6 does not always respect your time, but it will absolutely take your heart, stomp on it, and then distract you with a really nice explosion.

You will complain about it. You will swear you are done. Then you will queue for one more match.

I have mixed feelings. 

First of all, this game is definitely better than Battlefield 2042. For me personally, it’s also better than Battlefield 1 and Battlefield 5, mainly because I don’t really enjoy games set in World War I or World War II. I’m just not a fan of that period of history, so modern settings work much better for me.

The game still has a lot of serious problems.

The first and biggest issue is weapon progression. Upgrading weapons takes way too much effort. To fully level up a single gun in regular game modes, you need around 40 hours, which is just insane. The developers try to “help” by selling XP boosters, but honestly — do we really want to buy them? This system feels frustrating and unnecessary.

The second problem is the maps. About 50% of them are simply bad. Many maps feel unbalanced and are clearly designed either only for infantry or only for vehicles (or even worse for f* SNIPERS). Because of that, a lot of matches are not enjoyable at all.

The third issue is performance. Personally, I haven’t experienced major problems, but a lot of players complain that performance gets worse with every update. I also have a friend who has serious performance issues, so this problem clearly exists.

Another big disappointment is the Battle Royale mode. It’s bad, and I don’t even want to talk much about it. The real problem is that some Battle Pass challenges force you to play Battle Royale or other unwanted modes. That’s ridiculous. I don’t want to play those modes — so why am I forced to do it just to progress my Battle Pass?

I’ve spent around $100 and 200h on this game, and despite all these issues, I still have to say that the game is fun. I genuinely enjoy playing it, having Battlefield moments XD and I recommend it to my friends who already own it. I want to keep playing it.

I’d also really like to see a commander mode added to some game modes. Right now, a lot of players simply don’t know what they’re supposed to do. They just run around trying to survive — or worse, they don’t even understand their role. For example, players pick support classes and try to push the frontline alone, which usually doesn’t work.

Recently, I played Breakthrough, and our team was attacking from multiple directions. One side of the frontline was completely empty, so we could have easily pushed there and won. Instead, everyone was scattered all over the map, doing their own thing, and no one coordinated the attack. I even tried pushing one side on my own, but that obviously wasn’t enough.

If I’m not mistaken, Battlefield 4 had a commander mode. I don’t remember exactly how it worked, but I’d really like to see something like that again. I’m not even talking about being the commander myself — just having someone who actually knows how to play and can give directions to the team would already make a huge difference.

However, the community is slowly leaving the game — either because of these problems or others. The player count has dropped massively since release. Right now, it feels like less than 10% of the original player base is still active.

Hopefully, the developers will make the right changes so this game can survive and actually become something truly great. I really want to keep playing and enjoying it.

I came into Battlefield 6 cautiously optimistic.

I dipped my toes into Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V, but I didn't enjoy either of them for different reasons. Battlefield 1’s theme of World War 1 wasn’t my cup of tea and Battlefield V arrived deep into what I consider the “streamer era” of multiplayer shooters — faster, flashier, and less deliberate. The last Battlefield I truly invested time in was Battlefield 4 back in 2014.

Like many players from my generation, Battlefield 6 felt like it might be the long-awaited return to form and so I boarded the hype train.

Yet, after nearly 170 hours played — most of that within the first month — my feelings are overwhelmingly negative.

I know many modern gamers won’t agree with me but I come from a different era of shooters, and these are the reasons Battlefield 6 simply doesn’t make the cut.

[h1]Pacing Problems[/h1]
[h2]Maps: Smaller, Busier, and Less Battlefield[/h2]
Battlefield 6 launched with nine maps. Operation Firestorm is one such map but also a returning Battlefield 3 classic. Of the remaining maps, four feel extremely similar and notably small in scale.

This stands in stark contrast to earlier entries:

[b]* Battlefield 4 launched with 10 maps (23 total after DLC)[/b]

[b]* Battlefield 3 launched with 9 maps (29 total after DLC)[/b]

Each of those maps felt distinct. They catered to different playstyles, embraced scale and each had a character that fit the overall atmosphere of the game — a defining trait of Battlefield.

In Battlefield 6, most maps feel too small for Conquest, with Firestorm being the lone exception — and that’s only because it was designed during a different era. The developers appear to have prioritized minute visual detail over overall scale, flooding smaller arenas with assets, debris, foliage, and environmental clutter.

Since Battlefield 3, these games have looked good enough. The obsessive push toward hyper-detailed terrain like craters, grass, rubble, basically adding anything to a point of interests micro-detail really doesn’t improve gameplay. In fact, it actively harms it:

[b]* Vehicle play suffers by oversaturating barricades and other hurdles[/b]

[b]* Maps feel cramped not because there's actually focus on intriguing design but because each point of interest is so over-developed.[/b]

The time budgets in making maps are wasted on unnecessary visual noise.

Battlefield 3, 4, and even Battlefield 1 looked great not because they overstuffed maps, but because they stuck to strong themes and coherent atmospheres — [b]something Battlefield 6 sorely lacks[/b]. Seriously, what happened to Marine Corps. versus the People's Liberation Army or Russia's Armed Forces? Why must everything be focused on PMC's and other generic, rushed factions?

Modern texture quality, RAM usage, vRAM budgets, and compute resources don’t need to be blown on flashy, generic visuals. Ironically, that excess is exactly what makes modern shooters feel so bland.

[h2]Gunplay: Fast, Confusing, and Fundamentally Broken[/h2]
Battlefield 6’s gunplay is awkward at best and outright broken at worst.

SMGs dominate the meta and it's not just because of map size. The new attachment point system encourages hyper-specialization. In theory, that sounds interesting. In practice, it’s a disaster.

With the right setup SMGs and high fire-rate ARs become recoilless laser beams. Controller aim assist further exaggerates the problem.

It’s baffling this system wasn’t scrapped in favor of something closer to Battlefield 3 or 4’s simpler, clearer attachment design.

Adding to the frustration is the overwhelming number of settings. While customization can be good, there’s a point where moderation matters. The game throws so many sliders and toggles at you that it becomes unclear what actually needs adjusting.

Aiming itself feels wrong. I've had this strange blend of latency and stiffness with it. I play on mouse and keyboard, on a current-generation system (Core Ultra 7 265K, RTX 5070 Ti, 32 GB DDR5-6400, 4K60 display), and even after attempting extensive tweaking, aiming never feels as fluid or responsive as Battlefield 4.

Battlefield 6 is built around fast-paced gunplay, and while that initially sounded appealing, I quickly realized my reflexes aren’t what they were (skill issue) but what I deeply miss is the slower, more deliberate pacing of older Battlefield titles.

Weapon variety doesn’t help either. Guns feel copy-paste, differentiated mostly by fire rate. There’s little excitement in unlocking or experimenting with new weapons because none of them feel truly distinct.

[h1]Netcode Issues[/h1]
Battlefield 6 also suffers from poor netcode.

Hit registration and hit detection are inconsistent and unreliable. Portal was one of the game’s biggest selling points yet was borderline unusable for the first month and a half after launch. Connecting to matches was frustrating to the point of feeling broken.

For a feature that was heavily marketed, Portal launched in an unacceptable state.

[h1]Seasons, Battle Passes, and the Loss of Identity[/h1]
DICE today is not the same DICE from 15+ years ago. Most of the original developers are gone, replaced by new talent with fundamentally different priorities and the gaming industry itself has changed.

Gone are the days of buying a complete game that’s later expanded through substantial paid DLC.

For comparison: Battlefield 3 had five DLC packs, each adding four new maps. Battlefield 6 has re-released one map with a winter skin and added two new maps so far — one of which the community largely dislikes

More maps are “planned” via Seasons, but this drip-feed model feels like an excuse to deliver less content over a longer period of time.

Battle passes are another sore point. Locking weapons behind them is frustrating in a Battlefield game. Where are the weapon assignments? Where are the medals and ribbons? These systems were not just a method of progression, it was atmosphere and identity in a game that took itself seriously as a military FPS shooter. Their absence contributes heavily to my feeling that Battlefield 6 feels soulless.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
I gave Battlefield 6 a fair shot because many players from my generation were hopeful. But just months after release, the player base has dropped by nearly 90% and I am among those.

The initial excitement has faded into disappointment.

After 15 years of hoping to recapture the feeling of games like World at War, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, Battlefield 3, and Battlefield 4, I’ve accepted the truth that that era is long gone.

The players have changed. The developers have changed. The industry has changed. All of what it was before came together to create a golden era that simply cannot be recreated.

Battlefield 6 is not the Hail Mary we hoped for.

Forget the identity crisis of the prior Battlefield games. Battlefield 6 is a full-blown "Back to Basics" apology tour that manages to be both a tactical masterpiece and a glorious physics-defying circus. It’s the game where you can finally stop pretending you enjoyed playing as a "Specialist" with a grappling hook and go back to being a nameless Engineer who lives and dies for a single repair tool.

Here’s the current state of the frontlines as we head into 2026:
The "I’m Not a Hero" Class System: Classes like Assault, Engineer, Support, and Recon are back, meaning your teammates now have actual jobs they will probably still ignore in favor of trying to jet ram that enemy helicopter laying down suppressive fire.

The 64-Player Sweat-Fest: DICE ditched the 128-player "Where is everyone?" maps for focused 64-player carnage. Now, you don't have to run for 5 miles to find a fight; the fight will find you, usually in the form of a tank shell coming through a window you didn't know was destructible.

REDSEC Chaos: The new REDSEC mode is a high-stakes battle on the homefront that makes every match feel like a cinematic trailer, right up until a teammate spawns on you and immediately starts laying down light-machine gun fire behind enemy lines.

The "Frostfire" Grind: We are currently in the Season 1 extension, featuring the Frostfire Bonus Path. It’s a great way to earn cosmetics while questioning why you just spent four hours trying to get 150m headshots with a weapon that has the recoil of a startled mule.

Battlefield Labs: This is where DICE lets you play with "Experimental" ideas, like rebuilding the legendary Golmud Railway. It’s essentially a "Gray Box" experience where you help test the game so it (hopefully) doesn't explode when Season 2 launches on February 17, 2026.

Verdict: It’s the most expensive $400-million-dollar apology in history, and honestly? It’s working. You’ll come for the destruction and stay for the sheer absurdity of watching a building collapse onto a guy who was just trying to change his weapon class.

I cannot and will not recommend this game to anyone. I legit gave this game a chance and really wanted to love this one. Sunk almost 400 hours into this, and I'm done.  It's just frustrating and exhausting to play. I played every single multiplayer game mode, the whole campaign, leveled a ton of weapons, etc. 
      It's like the game has degraded, and is still in the process of getting worse since launch. It's not even the horrific slow leveling of weapons. Or the small crappy maps. Or the bad net code where you get shot around corners constantly. Or the most awful positional foot step audio in FPS history (it's actually laughable DICE won "Best Audio" award for this game). 
      Or the terrible Season 1 content. Or the ridiculous weapon balancing (SMGs with damn near perfect accuracy from across any map?). Or the insufferable player base. Nope...what absolutely 100% kills this game for me, to the point of uninstalling and not playing anymore? The scummy match making. 
      DICE took every note they possibly could with Call of Duty's manipulative, dirty SBMM and team balancing, and said "You know what?....we're going to implement an even more deceptive and underhanded version for Battlefield 6!" 

       l've played Battlefield 3, BF4, BF1, etc. I have also played 1000's of hours of Call of Duty over the years and experienced every version of SBMM in all these modern titles from Activision....and Battlefield 6 takes the crown for worst, most disgusting implementation I've ever seen. It's more prevalent in the smaller 8v8 game modes. If you have anything close to a 400spm, and 3.0-4.0KD....this game will absolutely make sure you're never winning a match again. They'll throw you a bone every once in awhile, but you'll be breaking out the largest backpack in gaming history to even barely squeak out your next win. 
      Just to give you an idea of how bad it is, I played a TDM match over the weekend on Mirak Valley and dropped 46 kills (out of a team of 8 people) 46 KILLS....and still lost 98-100. How does this even make any sense at all?  I regularly have to drop 30-40 kills in TDM matches to even get close to winning. Domination? I've had matches where I had 10 flag caps and 40+ kills and still lost. 
       Now onto the large game modes: Its even worse with the team balancing. EVERY SINGLE Conquest match ends in 12-15min, and is an absolute blow out. EVERY. SINGLE. MATCH ends with a score of 0-950 or it'll be 950-0 (or close to it). 
     Gone are the days of 45min to 1 hour Conquest matches where it comes down to each team fighting for their lives with only a few tickets left between each other. You're not getting that here. What you're getting here is a watered down version of "Conquest", that gives the illusion you're playing a "Battlefield" game. What DICE has done here is implement a "Come Back" mechanic, where it punishes a winning team by making them bleed tickets faster in an attempt to let the enemy team make a come back. Again....more deceptive and scummy team balancing. Whatever they implemented here, it's terrible and needs complete revamp. 
   This isn't the same DICE we all loved over the years that released legendary maps and game play to match. Nope, this is a whole different developer that took clues and hints from Call of Duty (a game which has basically cannibalized it's player base) and implemented them even worse here. Maybe visit this game in a year when it's been patched further and is heavily on sale.

The negative: 
-Most areas of the game are a noticeable downgrade from other entries in the franchise (with the exception of 2042). Atrocious map/spawn design combined with... 
...exploitable movement mechanics + inaccurate, inconsistent, insignificant, and sometimes contradictory weapon and attachment statistics/characteristics + whatever mess the current vehicle situation is (especially aircraft) + a general lack of balance...
...severely limits the potential for decision making and freedom in gameplay. 
-All around unintuitive and buggy UI/menus. Be prepared to spend a whole lot of time adjusting settings to make the game feel "right," but never quite getting there.
-Progression system is in dire need of some massive tweaking.
-Limited environmental destruction.
-Many major issues seem to be no more than one easy fix, but never find their way into the patch notes.
-Predatory monetization to pander towards the immature, profitable Fortnite community that BF6 wants, rather than the generally more mature community that it has. Cosmetically, all classes have lost their visual identity, outside of the gadgets on the player models' backs. That core community seems to be slowly but surely giving up on the game.
-Campaign isn't even worth mentioning.

The positive:
-Amidst all that, still offers a chaotic and cinematic experience, scratching an itch otherwise difficult to find in the genre today. 
-Good graphics and runs fairly well, though the current color palette and art direction of the game don't let the engine shine to it's highest potential. 
-Immersive sound design.
-Good framework for shenanigans with friends, if you have those. 

Could be a great purchase on sale, but hard to recommend to most people at full price anymore.

[b]DayZ is a hardcore survival game set in a post-apocalyptic open world, focused on realism, player interaction, and emergent stories.

✅ PROS

-Intense survival atmosphere – constant tension and immersion
-Meaningful player interactions – unpredictable encounters shape every session
-Large open world with freedom to play your own way
-Strong modding community that greatly expands content

❌ CONS

-Very steep learning curve and punishing mechanics
-Clunky movement and combat compared to modern titles
-Bugs and performance issues still appear
-Slow pace may feel boring to some players

🧠 Final Impression

DayZ delivers one of the most immersive survival experiences available, where every decision matters and no two stories are the same. However, its rough edges and slow gameplay can be off-putting.

👉 Recommended for players who love hardcore survival and emergent gameplay.
👉 Less ideal if you prefer fast action or guided objectives.[/b]

This game really sucks and it's unfortunate. I really wanted to like it. At least 70-80 hours of my game time is afk. This game feels very dated despite it being such a new game. 

Surely this wasn't the vision fully realized. The game feels unfinished. The gameplay loop is to fast travel (from your ship) to different planets, go to them and do something and fast travel again. In Skyrim, Oblivion, or Fallout 4 for example you had that continuity with a fully open map. Here there are many large spaces generated and it's great that the engine is capable of that, but none of them are connected so it is meaningless. If it was all one giant connected world it would have been more interesting.

I can use my imagination that I traveled with the ship and make myself believe it was all an open world. The gameplay loop and open world issue aren't even the biggest issues. 

The bigger issue is the game puts you into this world and this plot and just expects you to take it seriously. With the other games from Bethesda I could take them seriously because they were far enough out for me to suspend disbelief and enjoy the fantasy settings, even with fallout. Here I am dropped into this plot and expected to think it's cool, and believable. Also the characters really threw me off.

The blonde female is really annoying. She really took me out of immersion when she talked. Also seeing a bunch of characters with dumb college gen z hair cuts really threw me off and made it hard to take the game seriously. Even the voices of some of the characters and how they talk to you were really annoying.

I see where Bethesda was trying to go. An epic space RPG. Unfortunately it really just fell short. Maybe this game was just made 15 years too early, but I don't know. CyberPunk 2077 managed to pull off a way more crazy future feeling in a game that felt more space like and out of this world than StarField and it took place on earth. They didn't need to wait 15 years to make that game. Even Spore had a better space travel system and was more memorable and that game was made in 2008. The Creation engine is now capable of handling large maps but what is the point in having them if all you do is fast travel to them for no reason?

Look at the world map from Skyrim compared to this game. Bethesda could have made an EPIC and beautiful space map but they made a super bland and bad basic star map that makes me uninspired to explore.

Maybe Bethesda's game engine just needs some upgrades. I played some other space games recently and the combat, and space travel just feel was a lot better than StarField on all levels. Also It wasn't just a gimmick fast travel. Some of these games actually allow you to fly through atmospheres or accelerate 100000 thousands of times your speed to go to distant planets (or so it felt and showed). Unlike the fast travel system here with a lame map.

When the trappers guild recruiter first approached me and made it seem like an honor that I got a request to join the Trapper's Guild I can't tell you how dumb that moment felt to me. I was clearly supposed to think it was an epic moment that I got to join the guild but I can't tell you how much I just didn't care about their little guild. In Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim and least the guilds actually felt cool.

Also the dialogue in this game just really doesn't match anything I would want to say in real life, or in a game even roll playing a character. The language is all too flirtatious and flowery, and lame. Not all of us want to role play a 28 year old hipster from 2013.

Starfield a great space exploration game in the action RPG genre by Bethesda Game Studios of the legendary Elder Scrolls and Fallout series. I can recommend it to players that like decent first or 3rd person shooter combat and like progressing their character with skill trees. 

Pros:
- pretty tight shooter combat
- lots to explore, many side missions
- new game plus extends play time on one character, unlocking more Starborn powers and slightly increasing the challenge each time
- overall good graphics and smooth performance
- has base and ship building
- has space dog fights
- an excellent modding scene to change all sorts of aspects of the game and add new content, and if you're on PC, you can use Nexus Mods that has the largest number of mods

Cons:
- minigame to get Starborn powers gets old after a while
- random points of interest are well done, but there aren't that many, so you'll see the same ones over and over - they only vary by level of the system and which faction occupies the POI
- space travel is not seamless; there is a series of load screens when not fast traveling
- paid mods - Creations - vary a lot in quality and value for their price
- points of interest can be kind of far from where your ship lands

Note that there have been some improvements since launch, such as adding land vehicles and the company has promised more content.

I finally figured out what gives me the "uncanny valley" vibe about this game. Its the teeth. Everyone has the same teeth. All the faces are similar because they all have the same teeth.

The only reason I even have 48 hours in this mess, it's because I legit tried to start from scratch every time I got bored of it, in hopes it's peak my interest, but ... never happened. It has been since left uninstalled.

This is ... legitimately a below average game for being a "big studio triple-A" title. This doesn't even qualify as a "Bethesda game". Now, don't get me wrong, I enjoy some of their games, such as Skyrim, despite its flaws it's one of my all time favourites. The major problem is that everything that made Skyrim enjoyable for me is ... gone, in Starfield:

- World building is non-existing, and exploration is completely axed by a lazy map system with loading screens. Now I understand it's space and everything, but was it too hard to just ... make less planets and fill them with proper stuff to do? For example, Borderlands 3 did the planets system much better. You actually have things to do and explore, they're not just background, and they did not go over their heads with "space exploration in your ship". You CANNOT just pick a direction, walk, explore and find cool things. You look at a map, click planet, click destination, watch animation, wait for loading, you're there. Now you can MAYBE explore and just find the random spot 20 kilometers apart, conveniently shown already in your map.

- "Dungeons" (if you can even call them that...) are 99% just empty caves and abandoned facilities filled with Raiders. There's nothing. NOTHING. You just kill, pick the "rewards chest" and done. That's your dungeon. Now piss off. Rinse, and repeat. All the time. It's not even made interesting because of locations, everything is copy and paste. It all looks the same. And I thought Oblivion's dungeons were samey, this one takes the cake.

- Writing has been laughable since Skyrim, honestly, so I was not expecting anything. Writing is not something to play Skyrim for, but there are tidbits of something good here and there, it COULD be worse. And Starfield is that: worse. In everything. The characters are boring, the writing is so predictable and low effort, a children's book has more depth than this. I didn't expect it to be the greatest ever writing, but AT LEAST something good considering the time this game has been in development. But I guess until Emil Pagliarulo will be the lead writer, things can only get worse. Shame.

The only redeeming qualities of Starfield is the shooting (which is still far from great, but a good jump in quality from FO4), and to an extent the graphical presentation. I can't say anything, the game does thankfully look good, the art style is nice, and they seem to have done proper graphic updates to the engine, I can't deny that. 

But everything else both reeks of old and incompetent. Fallout 4 was already quite the dip in many aspects, but AT LEAST the gameplay loop kept it fresh, and the world building\design is actually fun, making Boston fun to explore and look at its many secrets.

Here? There's nothing like that. Just a mess of radiant quests, no real world building and design, boring "writing", uninspired everything.

I should have waited instead of pre-ordering it. This was my wake up call.

Just ... Forget it exists.

The truth is, it's some good casual fun. Kay and Nix are very charismatic, so just exploring around with them feels adorable. We get some of the star wars feel, but with some lightheartedness you'd get from the prequels. So don't come in expecting an Andor level gritty narrative against the empire, or some award winning gameplay, but if you find it for a low enough price, it's a nice past time to take some time away from competitive games.

Outside of that trademark Ubisoft performance issues, some repetitive gameplay design, outdated exploration and a large quantity of fetch quests, Star Wars Outlaws is one of my favourite action-adventure experiences in recent memory. I really fell in love with the story, the characters, several systems, world design, and a very true to promise recreation of the Scoundrel fantasy. When it gets running, Outlaws is at the top of its game, seamlessly weaving an engaging Star Wars underworld tale, with a high-stakes heist adventure. Set pieces and main story missions are fantastic, even if enemy encounters are disappointingly one-dimensional, and the endless typical Ubisoft platforming gets in the way. Combat feels thrilling, and tactical to a certain degree thanks to Nix, and smart permanent blaster pistol that offers quite a bit of versatility in playstyle. Unfortunately, for a game built around stealth, the systems are disappointingly barebones, relying on simple button takedowns, and few environmental elements. Massive's expertise with guns makes for great weapon design, that really allows for you to land on some choice weaponry throughout the game, which is why its confusing as to why they made a stealth-driven game. The game's four open worlds are a major highlight though. Impeccably designed, rich with detail, and full of things to do, even if they are largely fetch quests. It also helps that the game's (disappointingly) simple space flight sequences in the Trailblazer are made all the more engaging in space dogfights with overwhelming odds. 

Overall, a lot of Outlaws feels like wasted potential, a sad reoccuring tale within Ubisoft's many talented and skilled studios. But when it really puts its best foot forward, and commits to the Scoundrel fantasy, Outlaws remains one of my favourite Star Wars gaming experiences ever.

Star Wars represents a galaxy of endless possibility with thousands of planets, countless stories, limitless character potential. Outlaws takes this premise and funnels you through a linear, planet-locked narrative that wastes the IP's open-world potential. You're not exploring a living galaxy; you're moving through set pieces on rails.

The Protagonist Problem
Kay Vess embodies everything wrong with modern AAA character design: she's simultaneously unremarkable and inexplicably successful. She lacks the roguish charm of Han Solo, the earned competence of a seasoned scoundrel, or any real personality that justifies her meteoric rise in the underworld. She doesn't earn her reputation—she stumbles into it through plot convenience. Compare this to games like Cyberpunk 2077, where V feels like your character navigating Night City. Kay is just someone you're forced to watch make questionable decisions.
Shallow Systems Disguised as Depth
The game mechanics feel like checkbox features rather than engaging systems:

Minigames lack substance
The speeder feels like a theme park ride, not a vehicle
The economy is meaningless—credits have no weight
Customization is surface-level at best

It's the Ubisoft formula dressed in Star Wars clothing: pretty, but hollow.

What Actually Works (And Why It's Not Enough)
The presentation is genuinely solid—visually authentic Star Wars, excellent music, decent shooting mechanics and a cool slicing mechanic. The problem? These are the baseline features for a AAA Star Wars title, not selling points. A beautiful facade doesn't compensate for weak foundations.

The Rockstar Standard
This game needed the depth of a Rockstar production: meaningful choices, a living world with economic systems that matter, characters with actual depth, emergent gameplay that creates stories rather than following them. Instead, we got a nice looking game that plays it safe and delivers nothing memorable.

The Bottom Line
Star Wars Outlaws is visual spectacle without substance, a game that understands Star Wars aesthetically but fundamentally misunderstands what makes great games in this universe compelling. It's not broken, it's just aggressively mediocre in the worst way possible.

End of the line, its maybe worth it on sale if you're DESPERATE for Star Wars content. Otherwise, spend your money on another game.

reviews.review: Was skeptical when started playing this game. But over time this game really started to grow on me. Now when finishing up the DLCs it is really good fun. I can recommend it.

Knowing it was developped by the same dev as The Division 2, I had certain expectations for it, then saw the hate so I decided to wait it out before buying it. So when a major price drop arrived, I played the demo before making the purchase (which I highly recommend so you can get a better idea). I was NOT disappointed, the game is actually so much better than the demo, as you get the background story, dialogues, proper tutorial, etc. What I didn't expect was the space ship battles, which is a pleasant surprise.

Is it perfect ? No, it has its bugs but nothing that ruins the experience for me (I'm 15 hours in, as I'm writing this and haven't finished the game yet). The game crashed twice, but one of those times was because I tried the shift+tab to talk to a friend via Steam chat. This game hates overlaying stuff. Other than that, ennemies' AI is less impressive than The Division 2 during combat and when they ride speeders.

Is the game good ? YES !! At the price I paid for it, it feels like a steal. It's a fun adventure game with open world features where you play a thief trying to get by the only way she can. Some complain about the fact you can't be a ill intended criminal, but that's not the purpose of the game (it's not an RPG). See it more like RDR 2 (in character terms only) where you have a good person doing work for questionable people/criminals, as well as a certain level of choice when it comes to which criminal faction you want to be "friends" with. And that's fine with me as it allows for an actual story to be put into place.

I don't get the hate surrounding this game, besides technical issues (that only seems to affect my PC 5% of time time) and the selling price (but that's all AAAs).
Good game overall, you can either sneak or go in loud. Good lore and character cameos. Any star wars fan would enjoy this game.

Love the game, from the combat, skill progression, the characters and the story. The one and ONLY reason I'm giving this a dislike is because I lost my save for my ENTIRE playthrough up until this review.  It's acting like cloud saves aren't a thing at all, that even though I have cloud saving enabled my entire save and game settings are just ignored? I really do love the game but I have to hate on it for this one reason because you don't take away saves from players like that. We put so much time and effort into these save files it's like physically assaulting us it hurts so bad when it happens. If I go to reinstall my game again in the future and my save file DOES carry over then I will HAPPILY change this to a positive review! But until then the game gets this one. And before anybody comments I double and triple checked that cloud syncing was enabled. My save file persisted through a windows reinstall because of upgrading my PC and then this happens when I have an OS corruption and have to reinstall again? Hell no!
